chunk_findings.detail:
The stated policy has two independent leniency rules: (a) lenient outside the code tree (`config.py:256`) and (b) **the git‑ignored local layer is always lenient** (`config.py:318`). The change only implements (a): every layer returned by `config_paths(root, "gates.toml")` (which includes the local layer — see the `[:2]` slice used a few lines below to deliberately exclude it) is passed through a *single* `lenient = not _is_code_tree(root)` flag. When `root` is the code tree, that flag is `False`, so the local layer is parsed strictly and an unknown field there is a hard error, even though the identical layer is skipped for the main config.

Concrete failure: run ddflow from a checkout that `_is_code_tree` recognizes (the tree the code came from) with a machine‑local layer, e.g. `[gate.review] new_field = 1` in the local `gates.toml` (index ≥ 2 of `config_paths`). `overlay_table(..., lenient=False)` raises the unknown‑field error and *every* command fails, whereas `config.py:318` would have skipped the same field in the local layer of `config.toml`. The same single‑flag mistake applies to the one `overlay_array` call in `macros.py` and `companions.py`, which likewise cannot make the local layer lenient independently of the code‑tree check. So the bug B0016a65167 class of failure ("newer field written by a newer release on this machine") is only fixed for non‑code‑tree roots; it is not fixed for the local layer, which the policy says must always be lenient.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new tests inject the new-version field by writing `.ddflow/config.toml`:

    (root / ".ddflow" / "config.toml").write_text(text)

but `[gate.*]`, `[[macro]]` and `[[companion]]` are not read from `config.toml`; they are read from their own foreign files. The very same diff demonstrates this: the strictness test it modifies (`tests/test_gates.py`) puts `[gate.unit_tests]` into `.ddflow/gates.toml` to reach `load_gates`, and `tests/test_companions_verify.py` puts `[[companion]]` into `.ddflow/companions.toml` to reach `companions.load`. The docstring of the new file also draws the line explicitly ("config.toml's own sections are lenient … but gates, macros and companions still raised"): the target of B0016a65167 is the per-service files, i.e. the "foreign tables". Writing the fixture to `config.toml` therefore never feeds the code path under test.

Concretely, `_write(tmp_path, GATE)` followed by `G.load_gates(tmp_path, Config())` yields an empty gate map (KeyError `"unit_tests"` at the `gates["unit_tests"].command` assertion) rather than the expected warning-and-skip, and `test_in_the_code_tree_an_unknown_field_is_still_an_error` never reaches the strict schema, so `pytest.raises(ValueError, match="knob_from_the_future")` fails for a different reason. The same holds for `macros.load_macros(tmp_path)` and `companions.load(tmp_path)`. The regression test as written cannot fail on the unfixed code "because the loader refused the new gate/macro/companion field" — it fails because the field was never placed in the file the loader reads — so it does not establish the fix and should have been the probe for closing the bug as invalid.

chunk_findings.detail: The test now throws away the CLI exit code (`_code, out, err = run_cli(...)`) and asserts only that `"commmand"` appears somewhere in stderr. But the *unfixed* (strict) companions loader also reports the typo by name on stderr and exits non-zero, so every assertion in the test is satisfied whether companions became lenient or stayed strict. Concretely: revert only the companions half of the fix (leave gates/macros lenient, make `companions.load` raise again); `ddflow companions list --no-probe` then prints the `commmand` error and exits `FAIL`, `"commmand" in err` still holds, and `pytest.raises(ValueError, match="commmand")` (which is the *strict* path being explicitly forced with the monkeypatch) also still holds. The test therefore provides no protection for the companion half of B0016a65167 — the one CLI-level check of the new warn-and-continue behaviour is gone, and all that is left is the pre-existing refusal behaviour plus a direct strict call. To actually detect the regression the run must assert the successful exit (e.g. `assert code == 0`) together with the warning, so that a refusal fails the test.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten test no longer asserts that `companions list --no-probe` *succeeds* (the old `assert code == FAIL` was the only exit‑code check, and it has been replaced by `_code`). The new first half only checks `"commmand" in err`. On the unfixed code — where companions are strict for every root — the CLI does not skip the field; it rejects it, and the rejection message/traceback names `commmand` on stderr (the same stderr the new test greps). So given the very input of this test (a repo outside the code tree whose `companions.toml` has `commmand = "typo"`), the unfixed binary satisfies `"commmand" in err` and returns a non‑zero code that is now never inspected. The second half, `with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="commmand"): companions.load(repo)`, also passes on the unfixed code, because with the monkeypatched `_CODE_TREE` the strict‑everywhere loader raises exactly that error. The net effect is a test that is green before the fix, i.e. it does not "start with a regression test that fails on the current code" as the bug's fix protocol requires. chunk_findings.detail: The change turns a deliberately function-local import into a module-level one: `from ...config import Config, _is_code_tree` in `gates/defs.py`, `from ..config import _is_code_tree` in `macros.py` and `companions.py`. The original code fetched `_is_code_tree` lazily inside the loading function precisely because `ddflow.config` imports the service modules (directly, or via `services/__init__`) and defines `_is_code_tree` later in the module than that import point. That is exactly why `gates/defs.py` could already import `Config` eagerly (it is defined early) but had to defer `_is_code_tree`, and why `companions.py` had no module-level `ddflow.config` import at all. With the new eager import, a fresh interpreter that reaches a service module before `ddflow.config` finishes executing — e.g. `python -c 'import ddflow.services.macros'`, or any `ddflow` command whose import graph pulls in macros/companions/gates — executes `from ..config import _is_code_tree` against a partially initialized `ddflow.config` and raises `ImportError: cannot import name '_is_code_tree' from partially initialized module 'ddflow.config' (most likely due to a circular import)`. That aborts every command, including the out-of-tree invocation the fix is supposed to repair, so the regression test must be run in a fresh process (as the task requires) to avoid masking it behind an already-imported `ddflow.config`.

Concretely: revert only the companions half of the fix (leave gates/macros lenient, make `companions.load` raise again); `ddflow companions list --no-probe` then prints the `commmand` error and exits `FAIL`, `"commmand" in err` still holds, and `pytest.raises(ValueError, match="commmand")` (which is the *strict* path being explicitly forced with the monkeypatch) also still holds. The test therefore provides no protection for the companion half of B0016a65167 — the one CLI-level check of the new warn-and-continue behaviour is gone, and all that is left is the pre-existing refusal behaviour plus a direct strict call. To actually detect the regression the run must assert the successful exit (e.g. `assert code == 0`) together with the warning, so that a refusal fails the test.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_roborev_findings.py — `test_an_unknown_companion_field_is_refused_not_dropped`

chunk_findings.detail: The change turns a deliberately function-local import into a module-level one: `from ...config import Config, _is_code_tree` in `gates/defs.py`, `from ..config import _is_code_tree` in `macros.py` and `companions.py`. The original code fetched `_is_code_tree` lazily inside the loading function precisely because `ddflow.config` imports the service modules (directly, or via `services/__init__`) and defines `_is_code_tree` later in the module than that import point. That is exactly why `gates/defs.py` could already import `Config` eagerly (it is defined early) but had to defer `_is_code_tree`, and why `companions.py` had no module-level `ddflow.config` import at all. With the new eager import, a fresh interpreter that reaches a service module before `ddflow.config` finishes executing — e.g. `python -c 'import ddflow.services.macros'`, or any `ddflow` command whose import graph pulls in macros/companions/gates — executes `from ..config import _is_code_tree` against a partially initialized `ddflow.config` and raises `ImportError: cannot import name '_is_code_tree' from partially initialized module 'ddflow.config' (most likely due to a circular import)`. That aborts every command, including the out-of-tree invocation the fix is supposed to repair, so the regression test must be run in a fresh process (as the task requires) to avoid masking it behind an already-imported `ddflow.config`.

The change does not implement the fix it claims. The stated fix is "one `lenient_for(root)` policy passed into `overlay_*`" so that gates (`services/gates/defs.py:335`), macros (`services/macros.py:114`) and companions (`services/companions.py:268`) skip unknown fields outside the code tree. The entire diff consists of (a) an unused import of `_is_code_tree` into `services/gates/__init__.py` (marked `# noqa: F401`, referenced nowhere), and (b) a reworded docstring in `services/macros.py`. No `lenient_for` is introduced, no `overlay_*` call site is changed, and no strict/lenient branch is added at `macros.py:114`, `gates/defs.py:335`, or `companions.py:268`.

The regression test the workflow mandates ("Write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code") will continue to FAIL on this "fixed" code, so the bug is not closed. Additionally, the rewritten `macros.py` docstring now asserts a behavior ("elsewhere the file may be newer than the code, and the field is skipped with a warning") that no code in this diff provides, so the documentation actively misdescribes the running code.

The net effect is a test that is green before the fix, i.e. it does not "start with a regression test that fails on the current code" as the bug's fix protocol requires. The change's own bug description says `importer_harness.py:332` refuses anything over `max_chars`, and the original 600 cut existed precisely so the imported claim would clear that limit. So given a scraped research entry whose claim is longer than the enforced limit (e.g. a long paragraph under a `CONFIRMED` heading in `docs/RESEARCH.md`), `apply_import` writes a `research.recorded` event with an over-limit claim that the validator/harness refuses — the same failure B021a859d56 removes for memories, just relocated to research. chunk_findings.detail: The new expression `inside = any(path_in_glob(p, g) for p in landed for g in globs)` is evaluated *unconditionally*, before the `if led["done"]["files_known"] and globs and not inside:` guard. The original line `if led["done"]["files_known"] and globs and not conflicts(sorted(landed), globs):` relied on Python's left-to-right short-circuiting: when `led["done"]["files_known"]` was false, or when `globs` was falsy (e.g. `None`/absent, which is exactly why the `and globs` term exists in the same expression), it never touched `landed` or `globs`. After the change, the generator always iterates both. Given an input where the ledger's `files_known` is false (or a verification run with no declared globs) and `globs` is `None`, the old code fell through and appended nothing; the new line executes `for g in globs` on `None` and raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable` at line 221, aborting the verification instead of skipping the note. The retained `and globs` guard in the very next line is now unreachable for that input, which is the tell that the guard was defeated by hoisting the match out of the condition. (Same class of regression if `landed` is `None` when `files_known` is false, since `for p in landed` also runs unconditionally.)

chunk_findings.detail: The change claims to fix B1997c64c5a by replacing the prefix‑heuristic path test, but it never modifies the enforcement call sites: `globs_overlap` (`ddflow/core/schedule.py:186`) still implements the literal‑prefix rule, and `services/enforce.py:1260-1305` / `api/lifecycle/merge.py:432` are absent from the diff. The only edits are to `path_in_glob` (which already returned `False` for `("a.md", "a.md.bak")`), a behaviour‑preserving reformat in `verify.py`, and tests. Given the exact input of the new regression test — claim globs `a.md.bak`, then staging and committing `a.md` as `DDFLOW_AGENT=alpha` — the hook still reaches `globs_overlap("a.md", "a.md.bak")`, the prefix rule returns overlap, the commit is accepted, and the added test still fails. To close the bug, the coverage checks in `services/enforce.py` and `api/lifecycle/merge.py` must be switched to `path_in_glob`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new expression `inside = any(path_in_glob(p, g) for p in landed for g in globs)` is evaluated *unconditionally*, before the `if led["done"]["files_known"] and globs and not inside:` guard. The original line `if led["done"]["files_known"] and globs and not conflicts(sorted(landed), globs):` relied on Python's left-to-right short-circuiting: when `led["done"]["files_known"]` was false, or when `globs` was falsy (e.g. `None`/absent, which is exactly why the `and globs` term exists in the same expression), it never touched `landed` or `globs`. After the change, the generator always iterates both. Given an input where the ledger's `files_known` is false (or a verification run with no declared globs) and `globs` is `None`, the old code fell through and appended nothing; the new line executes `for g in globs` on `None` and raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable` at line 221, aborting the verification instead of skipping the note. The retained `and globs` guard in the very next line is now unreachable for that input, which is the tell that the guard was defeated by hoisting the match out of the condition. (Same class of regression if `landed` is `None` when `files_known` is false, since `for p in landed` also runs unconditionally.)

chunk_findings.detail: The reported false positive is "staged `a.md` accepted under a claim on `a.md.bak`", and the intent says the culprit is `globs_overlap`'s literal-prefix rule (`globs_overlap("a.md", "a.md.bak")` is true because `"a.md.bak".startswith("a.md")`), used as a path test at enforce.py:1260-1305 and merge.py:432. Those call sites are unchanged by this diff, so the commit hook still accepts the edit. Even if some caller did route through `path_in_glob`, this change still cannot fix the example: the pre-image returns `False` for `path_in_glob("a.md", "a.md.bak")` — `path == glob` is false, `"a.md".startswith("a.md.bak/")` is false, `fnmatch("a.md", "a.md.bak")` is false, and the glob does not start with `**/` — and the post-image also returns `False` (it hits the new bare-name branch `if "/" not in glob.rstrip("/"): return False`). So for input (`path="a.md"`, `glob="a.md.bak"`) the result is unchanged by the patch, and the added regression assertion in `tests/test_claim_path_match.py` (committing `a.md` under the `a.md.bak` claim must be refused) is not made to flip by anything in this diff. The fix is applied to the wrong function; the over-permissive caller(s) that produce the bug remain in place, and the new test still fails on the patched tree.

chunk_findings.detail: The memory path was fixed to refuse records over `[memory] max_chars` (dropping and counting them in `_memories_within`), but the research path has no equivalent length guard: `_imported_research` now returns `"claim": f.body` at full length, where the old code cut it to 600. The change's own bug description says `importer_harness.py:332` refuses anything over `max_chars`, and the original 600 cut existed precisely so the imported claim would clear that limit. So given a scraped research entry whose claim is longer than the enforced limit (e.g. a long paragraph under a `CONFIRMED` heading in `docs/RESEARCH.md`), `apply_import` writes a `research.recorded` event with an over-limit claim that the validator/harness refuses — the same failure B021a859d56 removes for memories, just relocated to research. The fix needs to filter/refuse over-limit claims and count them, as `_memories_within` does, rather than passing the body through verbatim and assuming only the verdict/probe validation matters.

chunk_findings.detail: `_leave_out_long_memories` now strips every over-limit memory out of `plan.found` at plan time, and the only place the "left out" tally is produced is the apply path: `kept, too_long, limit = _memories_within(repo, plan); _count_long_memories(counts, too_long, limit)`. For any plan produced by `plan_import` (the normal import flow), `too_long` is empty by the time this runs, because those records were already deleted from `plan.found` by `_leave_out_long_memories`. So `_count_long_memories` is a no-op and the `counts` key `memory over [memory] max_chars (N) not recorded` is never emitted, whereas before the change `counts.update(too_long)` always emitted it for exactly this flow. Concrete input: a repo containing one memory whose body is longer than `[memory] max_chars`; before the change the apply report contains the `... not recorded` entry with count 1, after the change the apply report's `counts` contains nothing for it (the information survives only as a transient `plan.notes` string). This contradicts the retained contract in `_memories_within`'s own docstring — "Counted, so the apply report says what was left out" — which is precisely the reporting the fix was supposed to preserve while it stopped truncating. The comment "A plan built by hand still gets the rule; `plan_import` already left them out" only covers hand-built plans; for the import flow the durable apply report silently loses the count that used to be there.

chunk_findings.detail: The new early-return block dereferences `module_tests` in the `G.verify_regression_test(..., tests=module_tests, ...)` call, but in this function `module_tests` is not bound anywhere above that point: the only place it can come from is the code that sits *below* the worktree guard, between the `tree = W.load_path(...)` / `if tree is None: return ...` lines (which the new block was inserted in front of) and the unchanged `if not base:` line at the tail used by the legacy path. That is exactly where the pre-existing code computes `base = fx.base ...` (the value this change replaces) and the test list, and no other line between `rec = st.bugs.get(bug_id)` and `fx = ...` exists that could produce it. Because an assignment anywhere in the function makes `module_tests` a local for the whole frame, the fast path raises `UnboundLocalError: local variable 'module_tests' referenced before assignment`. Demonstrated input: a fix task whose landing was recorded (`fx.landed_before` and `fx.landed_after` both non-empty — the ordinary post-merge state this change targets), then `ddflow complete <fix> --regression-test tests/test_importer_validators.py`; the branch is taken (`tree=repo`, `after=...`) and the crash happens on argument evaluation, before `verify_regression_test` is even entered, so the regression check fails with a traceback instead of returning `verified`/`could-not-run`. The guard placement is deliberate (it must precede the `if tree is None` early return because the worktree is gone after a merge), so the fix needs the test list bound above the fast path (or passed in) rather than below it.

chunk_findings.detail: `_case(repo)` returns the fix task's worktree (`wt`), and a git worktree cannot have `main` checked out while the primary checkout already has it, so `wt` is on the fix branch (or detached). The `pass_pipeline`/merge path records the pre-fix tree from the sha the task branched from (per the intent: "merge-base recorded at claim/worktree creation, or the first parent of the merge commit"), and that sha predates the `git add -A` + `git commit -qm always` that this test performs at lines ~32–35. So `tests/test_always.py` does not exist in the pre-fix tree at all, and the scenario the test claims to cover ("a test that passes [on the pre-fix tree]") cannot occur. Concretely, when the check runs `pytest tests/test_always.py::test_always` against the recorded base it gets a "file not found / no tests ran" error: if `_verify_regression` reads any non-zero exit as "fails on the pre-fix tree", the regression is accepted and `assert res.exit == 3` fails (res.exit would be OK); if instead it is treated as could-not-run, the assertion only passes because the reason string happens to contain "pre-fix tree", i.e. the test is vacuous and never exercises the pre-fix-pass refusal it is named for. To actually create a test that passes before the landing, `tests/test_always.py` must be committed on `main` *before* the fix branch/worktree is created, not added inside the fix worktree.

chunk_findings.detail: The diff does not contain the functional change it claims to make. The only edits to `bug_close.py` are two docstring hunks; `_verify_regression`'s body is untouched, so it still derives the "pre-fix" tree from the fix task's `base` (the branch NAME `main`, resolved at call time). Likewise the landed path in `mutation.py` still calls `verify_regression_test(..., tree=landed, base=base, ...)` with the same `base=base` argument; the only functional change there is appending `"tree": after` to the evidence dict, which records the post-fix landing commit, not the pre-fix source. The new docstring text ("A fix task that has LANDED is checked against its landing (`landed_before` is the pre-fix source, `landed_after` the fixed one), never the base by name") describes behavior that no code in the diff implements — nothing passes `landed_before`/`landed_after`, and the pre-fix tree is still built from `base`. Concrete reproducer from the intent: after `fix-B021a859d56` is merged, `complete ... --regression-test tests/test_importer_validators.py` still builds the pre-fix tree from `main`, which now contains the fix, so the test passes there and the bug is refused as "PASSES on the pre-fix tree" (or the tree is absent and it records could-not-run) — exactly the B0d5253d31f symptom. The described fix (use the sha the item branched from: recorded merge-base, or the first parent of the merge commit) is nowhere in this diff, so the regression remains reproducible.

chunk_findings.detail: The new early-return block dereferences `module_tests` in the `G.verify_regression_test(..., tests=module_tests, ...)` call, but in this function `module_tests` is not bound anywhere above that point: the only place it can come from is the code that sits *below* the worktree guard, between the `tree = W.load_path(...)` / `if tree is None: return ...` lines (which the new block was inserted in front of) and the unchanged `if not base:` line at the tail used by the legacy path. That is exactly where the pre-existing code computes `base = fx.base ...` (the value this change replaces) and the test list, and no other line between `rec = st.bugs.get(bug_id)` and `fx = ...` exists that could produce it. Because an assignment anywhere in the function makes `module_tests` a local for the whole frame, the fast path raises `UnboundLocalError: local variable 'module_tests' referenced before assignment`. Demonstrated input: a fix task whose landing was recorded (`fx.landed_before` and `fx.landed_after` both non-empty — the ordinary post-merge state this change targets), then `ddflow complete <fix> --regression-test tests/test_importer_validators.py`; the branch is taken (`tree=repo`, `after=...`) and the crash happens on argument evaluation, before `verify_regression_test` is even entered, so the regression check fails with a traceback instead of returning `verified`/`could-not-run`. The guard placement is deliberate (it must precede the `if tree is None` early return because the worktree is gone after a merge), so the fix needs the test list bound above the fast path (or passed in) rather than below it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/bug_close.py:316 (new landed fast path in `_verify_regression`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_case(repo)` returns the fix task's worktree (`wt`), and a git worktree cannot have `main` checked out while the primary checkout already has it, so `wt` is on the fix branch (or detached). The `pass_pipeline`/merge path records the pre-fix tree from the sha the task branched from (per the intent: "merge-base recorded at claim/worktree creation, or the first parent of the merge commit"), and that sha predates the `git add -A` + `git commit -qm always` that this test performs at lines ~32–35. So `tests/test_always.py` does not exist in the pre-fix tree at all, and the scenario the test claims to cover ("a test that passes [on the pre-fix tree]") cannot occur. Concretely, when the check runs `pytest tests/test_always.py::test_always` against the recorded base it gets a "file not found / no tests ran" error: if `_verify_regression` reads any non-zero exit as "fails on the pre-fix tree", the regression is accepted and `assert res.exit == 3` fails (res.exit would be OK); if instead it is treated as could-not-run, the assertion only passes because the reason string happens to contain "pre-fix tree", i.e. the test is vacuous and never exercises the pre-fix-pass refusal it is named for. To actually create a test that passes before the landing, `tests/test_always.py` must be committed on `main` *before* the fix branch/worktree is created, not added inside the fix worktree.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_regression_prefix_base.py::test_a_test_that_passes_before_the_landing_is_still_refused

chunk_findings.detail: The change does not implement the fix it announces. The intent states the repair is to build the pre-fix tree from the sha the item branched from (merge-base / first parent of the landing) instead of the moving base ref, and the added docstring in `bug_close.py` now asserts that "a fix task that has LANDED is checked against its landing (`landed_before` is the pre-fix source, `landed_after` the fixed one), never the base by name". But the diff's only functional edit is the evidence bookkeeping in `mutation.py` (`status, ev = verify_regression_test(...)` then `return status, {**ev, "tree": after}`); the call still passes `base=base`, and no hunk anywhere computes or forwards `landed_before` (or `after^`, or any merge-base sha). The body of `_verify_regression` is untouched — the hunk in `bug_close.py` ends at its docstring, and the next unchanged context line is `if not verify_regression:` — so whatever code "builds the pre-fix tree from `fx.base`" is still there. Concretely, for the scenario in the bug report: a fix landed on `main`, `base="main"`, `tests/test_f.py::test_f` fails only before the fix; after this change `base` still resolves to the post-merge `main` that already contains the fix, so the pre-fix run returns `passed`, `ev["prefix_outcome"] != "failed"`, the newly added assertion in `tests/test_regression_prefix_base.py` still fails, and the check still refuses a genuine fail-first test with "PASSES on the pre-fix tree". The added test therefore cannot pass on the code as diffed (except in the incidental `"/" not in ev["tree"]` respect), demonstrating that the described behavioural change is absent.

data.body:
Fixes bug B6797d49e48: tests/test_registry_publish_retry.py::_run sets MCP_CALL_TIMEOUT=1 for EVERY case ('every other call returns at once'), so a fake mcp-publisher/curl that takes over 1 s under host load (~160-200) is killed as a hang and retried: publishes/sleeps counts drift and test_duplicate_is_success_only_once_the_registry_confirms_it failed in 'ddflow ci run' for fix-B0d5253d31f (passes alone 3/3). Fix: a generous call timeout by default, the 1 s only for the hang case.

Write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code; then `ddflow complete fix-B6797d49e48 --regression-test <test>` closes the bug with the task (or `ddflow bug fixed B6797d49e48 --regression-test <test>` first).
data.title: Fix bug B6797d49e48: registry publish-retry test cuts off a slow fake publisher under load

data.claim: _run sets MCP_CALL_TIMEOUT=1 for all cases, so a fake call slower than 1 s (host load) is killed and retried, changing publish counts
data.falsifier: a fake publisher that answers after 2 s still publishes once with MCP_CALL_TIMEOUT=1
data.probe: test_a_slow_answer_is_not_cut_off_as_a_hang with call_timeout default 1 vs 20
data.probe_output: default 1: FAILED (504 retries, ::error:: not in registry after 6 attempts); default 20: 13 passed
data.question: Does the registry publish-retry test flake because every fake call is bounded at 1 s?

evidence.note: CONFIRMED: slow-ok case fails with a 1 s bound, passes with 20 s
brief read; test-only change, no source behaviour changes; workflow's real MCP_CALL_TIMEOUT (120) untouched
_run(call_timeout=20) default, hang test 3 s, new slow-ok fake word + test_a_slow_answer_is_not_cut_off_as_a_hang; 13 passed

Checked every _run caller: only the hang test needs a short bound (now 3 s, still under the 60 s subprocess timeout: hang 3 s + ok); worst-case suite time unchanged since fake sleep never sleeps; the step-shape test reads the workflow's own MCP_CALL_TIMEOUT (120), not the test override.
one parameter on the existing _run helper; no new helper

chunk_findings.detail: `test_a_call_that_hangs_is_cut_off_and_retried` runs `_run(tmp_path, "hang ok", call_timeout=3)`, which exports `MCP_CALL_TIMEOUT=3` for the whole process. That bound therefore also covers the second, non-hang call: the `ok` branch (`touch "$FAKE_DIR/listed"; echo "Successfully published"; exit 0`). Under the exact environment described in B6797d49e48 (host load ~160-200, fake publisher/curl calls exceeding 1 s), the `ok` retry can itself exceed 3 s, get killed as a hang, and be retried. The plan string only has two tokens ("hang", "ok"), so the third invocation exhausts the plan (the token selector matches nothing, the fake still appends to `$FAKE_DIR/publishes`) and the run ends with `publishes == 3` (or a non-zero exit from the unhandled branch), so `assert r["publishes"] == 2` fails. That is precisely the flake the change claims to eliminate, and it contradicts the change's own comment that "only the hang case asks for a short one" — the plan it uses pairs the hang with a call that is expected to return at once and should therefore run under the generous timeout. Setting the hang timeout to 3 only widens a margin that the bug report says was ~1 s under load, rather than removing the coupling between the hang timeout and the normal retry call.

chunk_findings.detail: `test_a_call_that_hangs_is_cut_off_and_retried` runs `_run(tmp_path, "hang ok", call_timeout=3)`, which exports `MCP_CALL_TIMEOUT=3` for the whole process. That bound therefore also covers the second, non-hang call: the `ok` branch (`touch "$FAKE_DIR/listed"; echo "Successfully published"; exit 0`). Under the exact environment described in B6797d49e48 (host load ~160-200, fake publisher/curl calls exceeding 1 s), the `ok` retry can itself exceed 3 s, get killed as a hang, and be retried. The plan string only has two tokens ("hang", "ok"), so the third invocation exhausts the plan (the token selector matches nothing, the fake still appends to `$FAKE_DIR/publishes`) and the run ends with `publishes == 3` (or a non-zero exit from the unhandled branch), so `assert r["publishes"] == 2` fails. That is precisely the flake the change claims to eliminate, and it contradicts the change's own comment that "only the hang case asks for a short one" — the plan it uses pairs the hang with a call that is expected to return at once and should therefore run under the generous timeout. Setting the hang timeout to 3 only widens a margin that the bug report says was ~1 s under load, rather than removing the coupling between the hang timeout and the normal retry call.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_registry_publish_retry.py (test_a_call_that_hangs_is_cut_off_and_retried / `_run(..., call_timeout=3)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The change raises the hang case's bound from 3 s to 10 s. The cut-off/retry this test asserts can only occur while the fake publisher's "hang" response is still blocking when the bound elapses; the fake itself is not modified by this diff, so its hang duration is coupled to the old bound. If the fake's hang is a bounded block chosen just above the previous 3 s bound (e.g. a 5 s sleep — the usual way a test double is written so it exceeds the timeout it was paired with), then with `call_timeout=10` the first call now returns normally before 10 s elapse, no retry is issued, and `r["publishes"]` is 1, so `assert r["publishes"] == 2` fails. The change multiplies the required hang duration by ~3.3x without lengthening the fake's hang or deriving it from `MCP_CALL_TIMEOUT`, so it silently drops the very behavior under test. The fix's own description ("the 1 s only for the hang case") also indicates the hang case is meant to keep the *short* bound; setting it to the largest value in the file contradicts that and makes the test wait a full 10 s for the kill.

chunk_findings.detail:
The old `_met` had a second rule, independent of stacking and unknown-dep policy: a dependency whose item is a `phase` is met when all of its non-abandoned tasks are DONE. The fix deletes that rule and delegates to `dep_status`, which per the author's own change only looks at the dependency item's own state. The result is that closing all of a phase's tasks no longer unblocks its dependents, and — worse — the roadmap contradicts itself: `_data` still counts a phase as DONE when `n_done == len(tasks)` (`done += 1; continue`), while `waits_on` for the dependent phase/tasks simultaneously reports that same phase as an unmet dependency.

Concrete input: the fixture `road_log()` without the newly added line, i.e. `g.done("T4", _ts(3))` with P2 a phase whose only task T4 is now DONE and no `item.completed` event for P2. Before the change, `_met(P2)` fell through `it.state == DONE`/`REVIEW+branch` to the `kind == "phase"` branch, saw T4 DONE, returned True, so P3/T5 landed in `## Next` (that is exactly what the unmodified test asserted). After the change, `dep_status(P2, cfg)[0]` is falsy because P2 itself was never completed, so `T5` becomes BLOCKED and P3 moves to `## Later`, even though `_data` has just classified P2 as DONE (counted in `done` and skipped from the lanes). The dependent therefore waits on a phase the same render reports as finished.

This is out of scope for B58010c24b3 (the report names only the review-with-branch rule and the unknown/typo policy), and the diff shows the smoking gun: `test_roadmap_phase_dependency_met_moves_phase_to_next` — whose name asserts precisely the behavior that was removed — had to be edited to inject `g.add("item.completed", "P2", {"kind": "phase"}, _ts(3))` for it to keep passing. Note that this edited test cannot serve as the required regression test either: under the unfixed code the added `item.completed` makes P2 DONE, so `_met(P2)` returns True and the test passes identically before and after the fix. So no test in this

chunk_findings.detail: Replacing `_met` with `dep_status` changes which phase dependencies count as satisfied, and the new rule contradicts the same function's own lane logic. The author's own test comment states the new truth: "Its tasks alone do not do it -- the scheduler waits for the phase itself." So after this change, `dep_status(P2)` for a phase whose tasks are all DONE returns "not met", while `_data` still computes `if (tasks and n_done == len(tasks)): done += 1; continue` — i.e. it drops that same P2 from the output as complete. Concrete input: the pre-existing fixture `road_log()` with only `g.done("T4", _ts(3))` (T4 is P2's sole task). Before the fix, `_met`'s phase branch (`kids and all DONE`) marked P2 met, so P3 landed in `## Next`. After the fix, P2 is counted DONE and omitted, yet P3 is emitted under `## Later` with `waits on P2`, i.e. the export reports a phase that depends on a phase it simultaneously reports as finished. The diff hides this by editing the test to inject `g.add("item.completed", "P2", ...)`; delete that line and the fixed code fails the assertion. Either the phase-completion rule must also be applied in the dependency check (keeping them consistent), or the phase lane rule must be changed so the output is self-consistent — as written, roadmap and `ddflow next` may agree while the roadmap contradicts itself.

chunk_findings.detail: The bug this fix addresses is described as a check-to-removal race: onboard "can delete a tree that an agent claimed *between its check and the removal*." That wording states the unfixed onboard *does* perform a check before removing; the defect is that the check and removal are not atomic (no log lock). This test performs no interleaving: it claims T1 first (`run_cli(repo, "claim", "T1", agent="worker")`) and only then calls `ON.apply(repo, [str(tree)])`. With the lease already present before `apply` runs, any check onboard already performs — even outside the lock — observes the lease and skips the removal, so the final `assert tree.exists()` holds on the *unfixed* code too. The test therefore does not fail on the current code as the task requires ("watch it FAIL on the unfixed code"), and it cannot distinguish the fix's central contribution (running `dispose_tree` under the log lock / atomic re-check) from the pre-existing non-atomic check. To actually regress this bug it would have to force the claim into the window between onboard's check and its removal (e.g. by interposing the claim before the removal call), which this test never does. If onboard in fact had no lease check at all, the bug would be a missing check rather than the described race, and then the fix's lock to describe would be untested regardless.

The old `_met` had a second rule, independent of stacking and unknown-dep policy: a dependency whose item is a `phase` is met when all of its non-abandoned tasks are DONE. The fix deletes that rule and delegates to `dep_status`, which per the author's own change only looks at the dependency item's own state. The result is that closing all of a phase's tasks no longer unblocks its dependents, and — worse — the roadmap contradicts itself: `_data` still counts a phase as DONE when `n_done == len(tasks)` (`done += 1; continue`), while `waits_on` for the dependent phase/tasks simultaneously reports that same phase as an unmet dependency.

Concrete input: the fixture `road_log()` without the newly added line, i.e. `g.done("T4", _ts(3))` with P2 a phase whose only task T4 is now DONE and no `item.completed` event for P2. Before the change, `_met(P2)` fell through `it.state == DONE`/`REVIEW+branch` to the `kind == "phase"` branch, saw T4 DONE, returned True, so P3/T5 landed in `## Next` (that is exactly what the unmodified test asserted). After the change, `dep_status(P2, cfg)[0]` is falsy because P2 itself was never completed, so `T5` becomes BLOCKED and P3 moves to `## Later`, even though `_data` has just classified P2 as DONE (counted in `done` and skipped from the lanes). The dependent therefore waits on a phase the same render reports as finished.

This is out of scope for B58010c24b3 (the report names only the review-with-branch rule and the unknown/typo policy), and the diff shows the smoking gun: `test_roadmap_phase_dependency_met_moves_phase_to_next` — whose name asserts precisely the behavior that was removed — had to be edited to inject `g.add("item.completed", "P2", {"kind": "phase"}, _ts(3))` for it to keep passing. Note that this edited test cannot serve as the required regression test either: under the unfixed code the added `item.completed` makes P2 DONE, so `_met(P2)` returns True and the test passes identically before and after the fix. So no test in this

chunk_findings.detail: `_met` short-circuits `dep_status` for any non-`removed`, non-`DONE` phase whose non-abandoned tasks are all `DONE`, returning `True`. That is exactly the "roadmap judges met with its own rule" divergence the bug is about, just narrowed to one case. Concrete input: `road_log()` with `P2` left un-closed and `T4` marked done (`g.done("T4", _ts(3))`), and `P3` waiting on `P2`. With the old code `waits_on` called `dep_status(state, "P2", cfg)`, which reports not-met because `P2` itself has not completed, so `P3` rendered under `## Later`. The removed test `test_a_phase_whose_tasks_are_done_but_which_is_not_closed_still_blocks` pinned precisely that behaviour and its docstring states "`next` waits for the phase itself to complete (its own pipeline), not just its tasks"; with the new `_met` that same input returns `True` and `P3` moves to `## Next`, so the roadmap once again disagrees with `ddflow next` for this input — i.e. B58010c24b3 is reintroduced rather than fixed, and the guard test that prevented the regression is deleted in the same diff. (The base docstring even asserted "the lanes and `ddflow next` agree (B58010c24b3)"; the rewritten docstring now openly concedes the exception, but an exception for a phase that is genuinely unfinished is a disagreement, not a representational nuance.) Note also that the phase's own lane under the stated lane rules ("DONE when its own state says so") is still not `DONE` in this scenario, so the comment "The lanes count such a phase DONE" is not what the lane logic does for the example above.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/kind_roadmap.py `_met` (lines ~35–42)

chunk_findings.detail: The change does not add a regression test that fails on the unfixed code; it edits the existing test so that it passes on both versions. The added line `g.add("item.completed", "P2", {"kind": "phase"}, _ts(3))` closes P2 before the assertion. On the pre-fix code, `_met` only takes its all-tasks-done shortcut when `it.state != DONE` (the `it.kind == "phase" and it.state != DONE` guard); once P2 is closed that guard is false, so `_met` falls through to `return dep_status(state, dep, cfg)[0]` — the exact call the fixed `waits_on` makes. So with this input the unfixed and fixed implementations are identical: P2 counts as DONE, P3's dependency is met via `dep_status`, and P3 appears under `## Next` with the `T5` row in both cases. Running this test against the pre-fix tree therefore passes, which contradicts the stated requirement ("write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code"). The actual behavioral change introduced by the fix — a phase whose tasks are all done but that is not closed is no longer treated as met, so its dependents move from Next to Later — is exercised only by the *unmodified* scenario (just `g.done("T4")` with no `item.completed` on P2), and the diff removes that assertion instead of asserting the new outcome (P3 in `## Later`). The fix as shipped is consequently unverified.

chunk_findings.detail: The new test asserts the "stacking off" semantics (`### P3` must land in `## Later`, i.e. a dependent waits for the phase itself to close) but never configures `[flow].stack` or `[schedule].unknown_dep_policy` — it just calls `road_log()` and `g.done("T4", _ts(3))` and inherits whatever the ambient/default config is. That config is exactly the axis B58010c24b3 is about: the report itself says the roadmap and `next` only "disagreed with stacking off". With `flow.stack` on, a phase dependency is satisfied once the phase's tasks are done, so `dep_status` reports P3's dependency met and the roadmap emits `### P3` under `## Next` rather than `## Later`; the substring `later` then contains no `### P3` and `assert "### P3" in later` fails (or, symmetrically, on a machine whose default happens to be "off" the test can pass without demonstrating anything). The test therefore encodes a stacking-off expectation while relying on the default, so its result is environment-dependent instead of being the regression test the bug requires. Setting `[flow].stack] = false` (and pinning `unknown_dep_policy`) explicitly is needed for the assertion to be well-defined.

chunk_findings.detail: The test records the lease *before* it calls the code under test: `run_cli(repo, "claim", "T1", agent="worker")` leaves a live claim in the log, and only then does `ON.apply(repo, [str(tree)])` run. Per the bug report, the unfixed onboard does perform a claim check — it merely performs it outside the log lock, i.e. the unsafe window is "a tree that an agent claimed **between its check and the removal**". With the lease already present when `ON.apply` starts, that pre-existing check sees it and declines to remove, so `tree.exists()` is still true and the test passes on the unfixed code — exactly the situation the task forbids ("Write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code"). The test therefore does not demonstrate the bug and cannot justify closing B5e83fb22cb; reproducing it requires an interleaving in which the lease is written *after* onboard's check and *before* its force-removal, which this test never creates (it is fully sequential). Note the module docstring's premise ("with no look at the leases") also contradicts the bug report's description of a check-then-remove race, so the test's stated mechanism is inconsistent with the defect being fixed.

chunk_findings.detail: The change does not implement the fix described in the intent. The lines that actually matter for B5e83fb22cb are unchanged context in this diff: `with log.transaction() if log else contextlib.nullcontext():`, `held = _held(...)`, and `C.record_removed(log, W.repo_root(repo), str(path))`. That means onboard *already* took the log lock, already re-checked the claim, and already recorded `worktree.removed` before this change; the only things this diff alters are how `EventLog` is constructed (extra `cfg.agent.id`/`log_cfg`/`lock_timeout_s` arguments) and the result label `"failed"` -> `"refused"`. Neither of those touches the race or the missing event. And the other path named in the bug report is not touched at all: `services/cleanup.py:322` is absent from the diff, so `cleanup` still removes a worktree without appending `worktree.removed` and without the log lock. Concrete failure: initialize a project, adopt a worktree to an item, then run `cleanup` so the tree is removed; no `worktree.removed` event is written, the fold still sees `item.worktree` pointing at the now-deleted directory, and a subsequent merge/flow that reads `item.worktree` operates on a stale path. The stated unification ("all four call one `dispose_tree`") is also not present — no such helper is added or called.

chunk_findings.detail: The added test cannot serve as the regression test the intent requires, because it does not exercise anything this diff changes. `test_onboard_apply_never_removes_a_tree_an_item_adopted` builds an adopted-then-released tree and asserts `tree.exists()` after `ON.apply(...)`. Whether that tree survives is decided entirely by `_held` (the adopted/standing-in guard) and the log lock, both of which are unchanged context lines in this diff. Given that the pre-change code already contained the lock, the re-check, and `record_removed`, this test passes on the unfixed code as well; only the newly added `outcome == "refused"` assertion in the neighboring test fails before the change, and that failure is caused by the string rename, not by the missing `worktree.removed`/race that B5e83fb22cb describes. So running the required "watch it FAIL on the unfixed code" step cannot be satisfied by this test for the actual defect.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_tree_dispose.py:75-92

chunk_findings.detail: The bug this fix addresses is described as a check-to-removal race: onboard "can delete a tree that an agent claimed *between its check and the removal*." That wording states the unfixed onboard *does* perform a check before removing; the defect is that the check and removal are not atomic (no log lock). This test performs no interleaving: it claims T1 first (`run_cli(repo, "claim", "T1", agent="worker")`) and only then calls `ON.apply(repo, [str(tree)])`. With the lease already present before `apply` runs, any check onboard already performs — even outside the lock — observes the lease and skips the removal, so the final `assert tree.exists()` holds on the *unfixed* code too. The test therefore does not fail on the current code as the task requires ("watch it FAIL on the unfixed code"), and it cannot distinguish the fix's central contribution (running `dispose_tree` under the log lock / atomic re-check) from the pre-existing non-atomic check. To actually regress this bug it would have to force the claim into the window between onboard's check and its removal (e.g. by interposing the claim before the removal call), which this test never does. If onboard in fact had no lease check at all, the bug would be a missing check rather than the described race, and then the fix's lock to describe would be untested regardless.

chunk_findings.detail: The new test asserts a *removal* behavior (`assert tree.exists()`) for an adopted tree, but whether that tree is removed is decided entirely by `_held(repo, cfg, log, path, item.branch)` and the surrounding `if held: return ...` / `W.remove(...)`, none of which are changed by this diff — they appear only as context lines. The only edited production lines are the `EventLog(...)` constructor arguments and the outcome string. Neither can change whether an adopted item's tree is removed, because the adoption check is inside the unchanged `_held` call. Consequently the test cannot be the required regression test: with the diff reverted, `ON.apply` takes the identical code path for this input, so the test either passed before the change too (if `_held` already honoured adoption) or still fails after it (if `_held` does not, in which case the fix is incomplete and CI is red). The bug report explicitly requires a test that FAILS on the unfixed code; this one does not exercise any changed behavior.

chunk_findings.detail: The stated bug is that *two* call sites, `services/cleanup.py:322` and `services/onboard.py:328`, remove worktrees without recording `worktree.removed`, so the fold's `item.worktree` goes stale, and the stated fix is that "all four call one `dispose_tree`". This diff contains no `dispose_tree` helper, no change to `api/lifecycle/merge.py`, `services/flow.py`, or `services/cleanup.py`, and only edits `onboard.py`. Therefore, if the report's premise about `cleanup` is correct, the defect it describes (after `cleanup` disposes a tree, the event log gets no `worktree.removed`, leaving `item.worktree` pointing at a deleted path) is entirely unaddressed by this change. At minimum the change does not do what its own description says it does.

chunk_findings.detail: The change drops *every* `rubber_duck`/`critic` failure whenever `gate is None`, not just review-finding failures. The stated requirement was to keep failures that indicate saturation — "timeouts, unavailable reviewers, infrastructure errors" — and remove only review-finding failures. `_outcome(ev)`/`_gate(ev)` carry no failure reason (the new code only sees `g in PR.REVIEW_GATES`), so a review gate that failed because the reviewer timed out or the vLLM server was unavailable is now silently skipped, exactly like a reviewer that returned findings. Concrete input: a wave where 6 of 12 chunk reviews time out under load yields 6 failed `critic` outcomes; `_failure_rate(..., gate=None)` `continue`s on all six, so `gate_failure_rate`/`gate_failure_ratio` stay at zero and below their `low` mark, and `flowcontrol` keeps stepping the parallel ceiling upward while the reviewer/pipeline is genuinely saturated. The signal that exists to detect reviewer overload now cannot see it. The fix needs to key on the failure kind (timeout/unavailable vs. findings) rather than the gate name, or turn the ratio off by default as the requirement allowed, instead of asserting every review-gate failure is a finding.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/flowsignals.py:155 (`_failure_rate`)

chunk_findings.detail: The bug this fix addresses is described as a check-to-removal race: onboard "can delete a tree that an agent claimed *between its check and the removal*." That wording states the unfixed onboard *does* perform a check before removing; the defect is that the check and removal are not atomic (no log lock). This test performs no interleaving: it claims T1 first (`run_cli(repo, "claim", "T1", agent="worker")`) and only then calls `ON.apply(repo, [str(tree)])`. With the lease already present before `apply` runs, any check onboard already performs — even outside the lock — observes the lease and skips the removal, so the final `assert tree.exists()` holds on the *unfixed* code too. The test therefore does not fail on the current code as the task requires ("watch it FAIL on the unfixed code"), and it cannot distinguish the fix's central contribution (running `dispose_tree` under the log lock / atomic re-check) from the pre-existing non-atomic check. To actually regress this bug it would have to force the claim into the window between onboard's check and its removal (e.g. by interposing the claim before the removal call), which this test never does. If onboard in fact had no lease check at all, the bug would be a missing check rather than the described race, and then the fix's lock to describe would be untested regardless.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_tree_dispose.py:test_onboard_apply_never_removes_a_tree_an_agent_holds

chunk_findings.detail: The new test asserts a *removal* behavior (`assert tree.exists()`) for an adopted tree, but whether that tree is removed is decided entirely by `_held(repo, cfg, log, path, item.branch)` and the surrounding `if held: return ...` / `W.remove(...)`, none of which are changed by this diff — they appear only as context lines. The only edited production lines are the `EventLog(...)` constructor arguments and the outcome string. Neither can change whether an adopted item's tree is removed, because the adoption check is inside the unchanged `_held` call. Consequently the test cannot be the required regression test: with the diff reverted, `ON.apply` takes the identical code path for this input, so the test either passed before the change too (if `_held` already honoured adoption) or still fails after it (if `_held` does not, in which case the fix is incomplete and CI is red). The bug report explicitly requires a test that FAILS on the unfixed code; this one does not exercise any changed behavior.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_tree_dispose.py:73 (test_onboard_apply_never_removes_a_tree_an_item_adopted)

chunk_findings.detail: The stated bug is that *two* call sites, `services/cleanup.py:322` and `services/onboard.py:328`, remove worktrees without recording `worktree.removed`, so the fold's `item.worktree` goes stale, and the stated fix is that "all four call one `dispose_tree`". This diff contains no `dispose_tree` helper, no change to `api/lifecycle/merge.py`, `services/flow.py`, or `services/cleanup.py`, and only edits `onboard.py`. Therefore, if the report's premise about `cleanup` is correct, the defect it describes (after `cleanup` disposes a tree, the event log gets no `worktree.removed`, leaving `item.worktree` pointing at a deleted path) is entirely unaddressed by this change. At minimum the change does not do what its own description says it does.
chunk_findings.title: services/cleanup.py:322 (incomplete fix)

chunk_findings.detail: The diff only swaps the agent id used to construct one `EventLog`. It does not implement the fix the intent claims: nothing adds the log lock, the post-check claim re-check, or the `worktree.removed` logging around onboard's removal, and `cleanup.py` is not touched at all. Given the bug description ("onboard also removes with force and without the log lock, so it can delete a tree that an agent claimed between its check and the removal"), the race is still live in this change: release tree T, invoke onboard on T, and have another process claim/lease T in the window between onboard's existence check and its force removal — onboard still deletes T, leaving the claimant with a lease pointing at a deleted worktree. The changed line cannot affect that interleaving. Likewise the stated stale-fold symptom for cleanup (`cleanup.py:322` never logs `worktree.removed`) is untouched, so a tree removed by `ddflow cleanup` still leaves `fold`'s `item.worktree` pointing at the removed path. Closing B5e83fb22cb on this diff is premature.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/onboard.py:368 (the `effective_agent_id` change) / ddflow/services/onboard.py:328 (untouched removal path)

chunk_findings.detail: The added "regression test" does not exercise the bug it is supposed to guard. Its only assertion is `removed[-1].agent == "sweeper-7"`, i.e., that the `DDFLOW_AGENT` value is propagated into the removal event's agent field. It contains no check that the removal happened under the log lock, that the claim was re-checked, or that `fold`'s `item.worktree` was cleared. Input that demonstrates the gap: run this test on a build where onboard removes a tree that another process claimed mid-flight (or where cleanup removes a tree and never emits `worktree.removed`) — the agent-attribution assertion is unaffected, so the test passes while the reported defect is still present. It therefore cannot serve as the failing-then-passing regression test for B5e83fb22cb; at most it pins the incidental `effective_agent_id` behavior.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_tree_dispose.py:95 `test_the_removal_is_written_as_the_agent_ddflow_agent_names`

chunk_findings.detail: The test records the lease *before* it calls the code under test: `run_cli(repo, "claim", "T1", agent="worker")` leaves a live claim in the log, and only then does `ON.apply(repo, [str(tree)])` run. Per the bug report, the unfixed onboard does perform a claim check — it merely performs it outside the log lock, i.e. the unsafe window is "a tree that an agent claimed **between its check and the removal**". With the lease already present when `ON.apply` starts, that pre-existing check sees it and declines to remove, so `tree.exists()` is still true and the test passes on the unfixed code — exactly the situation the task forbids ("Write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code"). The test therefore does not demonstrate the bug and cannot justify closing B5e83fb22cb; reproducing it requires an interleaving in which the lease is written *after* onboard's check and *before* its force-removal, which this test never creates (it is fully sequential). Note the module docstring's premise ("with no look at the leases") also contradicts the bug report's description of a check-then-remove race, so the test's stated mechanism is inconsistent with the defect being fixed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_tree_dispose.py:66 — `test_onboard_apply_never_removes_a_tree_an_agent_holds`

chunk_findings.detail: The change does not implement the fix described in the intent. The lines that actually matter for B5e83fb22cb are unchanged context in this diff: `with log.transaction() if log else contextlib.nullcontext():`, `held = _held(...)`, and `C.record_removed(log, W.repo_root(repo), str(path))`. That means onboard *already* took the log lock, already re-checked the claim, and already recorded `worktree.removed` before this change; the only things this diff alters are how `EventLog` is constructed (extra `cfg.agent.id`/`log_cfg`/`lock_timeout_s` arguments) and the result label `"failed"` -> `"refused"`. Neither of those touches the race or the missing event. And the other path named in the bug report is not touched at all: `services/cleanup.py:322` is absent from the diff, so `cleanup` still removes a worktree without appending `worktree.removed` and without the log lock. Concrete failure: initialize a project, adopt a worktree to an item, then run `cleanup` so the tree is removed; no `worktree.removed` event is written, the fold still sees `item.worktree` pointing at the now-deleted directory, and a subsequent merge/flow that reads `item.worktree` operates on a stale path. The stated unification ("all four call one `dispose_tree`") is also not present — no such helper is added or called.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/onboard.py:365-380

chunk_findings.detail: The added test cannot serve as the regression test the intent requires, because it does not exercise anything this diff changes. `test_onboard_apply_never_removes_a_tree_an_item_adopted` builds an adopted-then-released tree and asserts `tree.exists()` after `ON.apply(...)`. Whether that tree survives is decided entirely by `_held` (the adopted/standing-in guard) and the log lock, both of which are unchanged context lines in this diff. Given that the pre-change code already contained the lock, the re-check, and `record_removed`, this test passes on the unfixed code as well; only the newly added `outcome == "refused"` assertion in the neighboring test fails before the change, and that failure is caused by the string rename, not by the missing `worktree.removed`/race that B5e83fb22cb describes. So running the required "watch it FAIL on the unfixed code" step cannot be satisfied by this test for the actual defect.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_tree_dispose.py:75-92

chunk_findings.detail: The stated bug requires that the *cleanup* path also emit `worktree.removed`; the intent says "cleanup (services/cleanup.py:322) and onboard (services/onboard.py:328) do not [log], so the fold's item.worktree stays stale." The diff is declared complete ("part 1 of 1") yet contains changes only to `services/onboard.py` (one line) and `tests/test_tree_dispose.py`. No hunk touches `services/cleanup.py`. Concretely: release a tree, run `cleanup` on it, then `fold` — the removal still produces no `worktree.removed` event, so `item.worktree` remains pointing at a tree that no longer exists. The exact symptom named in B5e83fb22cb is therefore not fixed for the cleanup code path. The new test cannot catch this because it only exercises `ON.apply` and only checks the event's `agent` field.
chunk_findings.title: services/cleanup.py (no hunk in diff)

chunk_findings.detail: The only functional change in `onboard.py` is the `EventLog` constructor argument (`cfg.agent.id or ""` → `effective_agent_id(repo, cfg)`). The intent describes the onboard defect as: it "removes with force and without the log lock, so it can delete a tree that an agent claimed between its check and the removal," and states the fix must "run under the log lock, re-check the claim, apply the adopted/standing-in guards." None of that logic appears anywhere in the diff — there is a single hunk in `onboard.py`, and it touches only the agent-id argument of an `EventLog` that is unrelated to the claimed re-check/lock/guard work. Interleaving that still defeats the change: `onboard` observes the tree as disposable, an agent claims it (`release`/claim succeeds) before `onboard`'s removal executes, and `onboard` still force-removes it, because the removal site was not moved under the log lock nor made to re-check the claim. The added regression test does not exercise this path (it asserts only `removed[-1].agent == "sweeper-7"`), so the race described in the bug report remains reachable after this change.
chunk_findings.title: services/onboard.py:368

chunk_findings.detail: The fixture injects `"gate_failure_ratio": 1.6`, but the bug report this test is derived from states the low mark for that signal is 1.5. So 1.6 is *above* the low mark, i.e. an active "reduce the limit" value (which is why it can be the signal that holds the limit), not "its neutral band" as the docstring claims. The reported incident is precisely the harder case: the ratio hovered at 1.2–1.6 with the mark at 1.5, i.e. mostly **below** the mark (1.2–1.4), where the signal blocks growth (holds the limit) without ever triggering a decrease of its own, so a "latest decision" that only remembers the last signal that *caused a decrease* still names the null `reviewer_latency_ratio`. Given the fixture as written, an implementation that attributes `limited_by` only to signals that actively lowered the limit passes `d.limited_by == "gate_failure_ratio"` here, while the observed symptom (status says "limited by reviewer latency ratio" with a null ratio) reappears for any sample where `gate_failure_ratio` sits below 1.5. To reproduce the incident, the 120-sample block should use a value below the low mark (e.g. 1.2–1.4), not 1.6.
