chunk_findings.detail: The test records the lease *before* it calls the code under test: `run_cli(repo, "claim", "T1", agent="worker")` leaves a live claim in the log, and only then does `ON.apply(repo, [str(tree)])` run. Per the bug report, the unfixed onboard does perform a claim check — it merely performs it outside the log lock, i.e. the unsafe window is "a tree that an agent claimed **between its check and the removal**". With the lease already present when `ON.apply` starts, that pre-existing check sees it and declines to remove, so `tree.exists()` is still true and the test passes on the unfixed code — exactly the situation the task forbids ("Write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code"). The test therefore does not demonstrate the bug and cannot justify closing B5e83fb22cb; reproducing it requires an interleaving in which the lease is written *after* onboard's check and *before* its force-removal, which this test never creates (it is fully sequential). Note the module docstring's premise ("with no look at the leases") also contradicts the bug report's description of a check-then-remove race, so the test's stated mechanism is inconsistent with the defect being fixed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_tree_dispose.py:66 — `test_onboard_apply_never_removes_a_tree_an_agent_holds`

chunk_findings.detail: The change does not implement the fix described in the intent. The lines that actually matter for B5e83fb22cb are unchanged context in this diff: `with log.transaction() if log else contextlib.nullcontext():`, `held = _held(...)`, and `C.record_removed(log, W.repo_root(repo), str(path))`. That means onboard *already* took the log lock, already re-checked the claim, and already recorded `worktree.removed` before this change; the only things this diff alters are how `EventLog` is constructed (extra `cfg.agent.id`/`log_cfg`/`lock_timeout_s` arguments) and the result label `"failed"` -> `"refused"`. Neither of those touches the race or the missing event. And the other path named in the bug report is not touched at all: `services/cleanup.py:322` is absent from the diff, so `cleanup` still removes a worktree without appending `worktree.removed` and without the log lock. Concrete failure: initialize a project, adopt a worktree to an item, then run `cleanup` so the tree is removed; no `worktree.removed` event is written, the fold still sees `item.worktree` pointing at the now-deleted directory, and a subsequent merge/flow that reads `item.worktree` operates on a stale path. The stated unification ("all four call one `dispose_tree`") is also not present — no such helper is added or called.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/onboard.py:365-380

chunk_findings.detail: The added test cannot serve as the regression test the intent requires, because it does not exercise anything this diff changes. `test_onboard_apply_never_removes_a_tree_an_item_adopted` builds an adopted-then-released tree and asserts `tree.exists()` after `ON.apply(...)`. Whether that tree survives is decided entirely by `_held` (the adopted/standing-in guard) and the log lock, both of which are unchanged context lines in this diff. Given that the pre-change code already contained the lock, the re-check, and `record_removed`, this test passes on the unfixed code as well; only the newly added `outcome == "refused"` assertion in the neighboring test fails before the change, and that failure is caused by the string rename, not by the missing `worktree.removed`/race that B5e83fb22cb describes. So running the required "watch it FAIL on the unfixed code" step cannot be satisfied by this test for the actual defect.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_tree_dispose.py:75-92

chunk_findings.detail: The stated bug requires that the *cleanup* path also emit `worktree.removed`; the intent says "cleanup (services/cleanup.py:322) and onboard (services/onboard.py:328) do not [log], so the fold's item.worktree stays stale." The diff is declared complete ("part 1 of 1") yet contains changes only to `services/onboard.py` (one line) and `tests/test_tree_dispose.py`. No hunk touches `services/cleanup.py`. Concretely: release a tree, run `cleanup` on it, then `fold` — the removal still produces no `worktree.removed` event, so `item.worktree` remains pointing at a tree that no longer exists. The exact symptom named in B5e83fb22cb is therefore not fixed for the cleanup code path. The new test cannot catch this because it only exercises `ON.apply` and only checks the event's `agent` field.
chunk_findings.title: services/cleanup.py (no hunk in diff)

chunk_findings.detail: The only functional change in `onboard.py` is the `EventLog` constructor argument (`cfg.agent.id or ""` → `effective_agent_id(repo, cfg)`). The intent describes the onboard defect as: it "removes with force and without the log lock, so it can delete a tree that an agent claimed between its check and the removal," and states the fix must "run under the log lock, re-check the claim, apply the adopted/standing-in guards." None of that logic appears anywhere in the diff — there is a single hunk in `onboard.py`, and it touches only the agent-id argument of an `EventLog` that is unrelated to the claimed re-check/lock/guard work. Interleaving that still defeats the change: `onboard` observes the tree as disposable, an agent claims it (`release`/claim succeeds) before `onboard`'s removal executes, and `onboard` still force-removes it, because the removal site was not moved under the log lock nor made to re-check the claim. The added regression test does not exercise this path (it asserts only `removed[-1].agent == "sweeper-7"`), so the race described in the bug report remains reachable after this change.
chunk_findings.title: services/onboard.py:368

chunk_findings.detail: The change is *only* agent plumbing: it threads a new `agent` argument through `preflight` → `apply` → `_remove_worktree` so the `EventLog` gets `--agent` instead of only `DDFLOW_AGENT`/`[agent].id`. It does not contain any of the mechanisms the stated fix depends on. There is no shared `dispose_tree`, no acquisition of the log lock around the actual `W.remove(..., force=True)` call, and no re-check of the claim inside `_remove_worktree`. The race called out in the bug therefore remains directly reproducible: `apply` folds the log and selects `item` as removable, then in the window before `_remove_worktree` runs, agent A claims that worktree; because `_remove_worktree` still removes with force and never re-reads the claim under the lock, A's just-claimed tree is deleted. The new test `test_the_removal_is_written_as_the_declared_agent` does not exercise this interleaving at all — it only asserts that the `worktree.removed` event's `agent` field equals `"declared-3"` — so `ddflow complete fix-B5e83fb22cb --regression-test <test>` can close the bug while the force-remove race is still live.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/onboard.py:_remove_worktree (with ddflow/api/onboard.py:preflight)

chunk_findings.detail: The stated bug has two halves ("cleanup and onboard remove worktrees without recording worktree.removed"), and the stated fix is that *all four* call sites (merge, flow, cleanup, onboard) route through one `dispose_tree`. No file named `cleanup.py` (nor `merge.py`/`flow.py`) appears in this diff at all; the only production changes are in `api/onboard.py` and `services/onboard.py`. Concretely, running `cleanup` against a repo containing a merged leftover worktree still deletes that tree without appending a `worktree.removed` event, so the fold's `item.worktree` remains stale after cleanup — the exact symptom the bug reports, and one the added test (which only runs the `onboard` preflight path) cannot detect.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup.py (not present in the diff)

chunk_findings.detail: The fixture injects `"gate_failure_ratio": 1.6`, but the bug report this test is derived from states the low mark for that signal is 1.5. So 1.6 is *above* the low mark, i.e. an active "reduce the limit" value (which is why it can be the signal that holds the limit), not "its neutral band" as the docstring claims. The reported incident is precisely the harder case: the ratio hovered at 1.2–1.6 with the mark at 1.5, i.e. mostly **below** the mark (1.2–1.4), where the signal blocks growth (holds the limit) without ever triggering a decrease of its own, so a "latest decision" that only remembers the last signal that *caused a decrease* still names the null `reviewer_latency_ratio`. Given the fixture as written, an implementation that attributes `limited_by` only to signals that actively lowered the limit passes `d.limited_by == "gate_failure_ratio"` here, while the observed symptom (status says "limited by reviewer latency ratio" with a null ratio) reappears for any sample where `gate_failure_ratio` sits below 1.5. To reproduce the incident, the 120-sample block should use a value below the low mark (e.g. 1.2–1.4), not 1.6.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_flow_overload_semantics.py:test_limited_by_never_names_a_signal_that_is_null_now

chunk_findings.detail: Requirement (2) of B767745dee6 is not implemented anywhere in this change: nothing in the diff touches how `gate_failure_ratio` is computed, so review-finding failures still count toward it. The reported symptom therefore persists. Feed the incident's own samples: `gate_failure_ratio = 1.6` produced by a refactoring-phase review gate (no timeouts/unavailable reviewers) and `reviewer_latency_ratio = None`. With the patched code the fallback still selects `gate_failure_ratio` (the change only adds the helper call; the fallback path that names over-low signals is unchanged), so `limited_by == "gate_failure_ratio"` and growth is still held, exactly the condition the bug says must not hold ("failed review gates mean the reviewer found issues, not that capacity is short"). The change is cosmetic: it only relabels the reason. The new test itself encodes this: `assert _after_a_decrease(None, 1.6).limited_by == "gate_failure_ratio"` asserts that a review-finding ratio above the 1.5 low mark is the limiter, i.e. it pins the unfixed behavior as expected.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/flowcontrol.py:295 (`elif _still_over_low(...)` branch) / tests/test_flow_overload_semantics.py

chunk_findings.detail: This test cannot be the regression test for the bug, and it does not cover the bug's stated condition. The bug scenario is "the reason names a signal that is null now". The old condition already excluded null: `st.dec_signal and ring[-1].signals.get(st.dec_signal) is not None` is False when `reviewer_latency_ratio` is None, so control already fell through to the branch that names the real limiter. The new condition (`_still_over_low` → `v is None` → False) takes the identical path. Concretely, for `rlr=None, gfr=1.6` both the pre-image and post-image code produce `limited_by == "gate_failure_ratio"`; the pre-image version of this very test asserted that same equality. So the test passes before and after the change — it cannot "fail on the unfixed code" as required, and a regression that reintroduces the null-naming behavior would not be caught. The only test that actually distinguishes old from new is `test_a_decrease_signal_that_recovered_is_not_named`, which exercises a *non-null, below-low* ratio (`rlr=1.0`), not the null case described in the bug; that path was already handled by the old guard, so the bug's actual input is neither fixed nor guarded.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_flow_overload_semantics.py (`test_limited_by_never_names_a_signal_that_is_null_now`)

chunk_findings.detail: The bug this fix addresses is described as a check-to-removal race: onboard "can delete a tree that an agent claimed *between its check and the removal*." That wording states the unfixed onboard *does* perform a check before removing; the defect is that the check and removal are not atomic (no log lock). This test performs no interleaving: it claims T1 first (`run_cli(repo, "claim", "T1", agent="worker")`) and only then calls `ON.apply(repo, [str(tree)])`. With the lease already present before `apply` runs, any check onboard already performs — even outside the lock — observes the lease and skips the removal, so the final `assert tree.exists()` holds on the *unfixed* code too. The test therefore does not fail on the current code as the task requires ("watch it FAIL on the unfixed code"), and it cannot distinguish the fix's central contribution (running `dispose_tree` under the log lock / atomic re-check) from the pre-existing non-atomic check. To actually regress this bug it would have to force the claim into the window between onboard's check and its removal (e.g. by interposing the claim before the removal call), which this test never does. If onboard in fact had no lease check at all, the bug would be a missing check rather than the described race, and then the fix's lock to describe would be untested regardless.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_tree_dispose.py:test_onboard_apply_never_removes_a_tree_an_agent_holds

chunk_findings.detail: The new test asserts a *removal* behavior (`assert tree.exists()`) for an adopted tree, but whether that tree is removed is decided entirely by `_held(repo, cfg, log, path, item.branch)` and the surrounding `if held: return ...` / `W.remove(...)`, none of which are changed by this diff — they appear only as context lines. The only edited production lines are the `EventLog(...)` constructor arguments and the outcome string. Neither can change whether an adopted item's tree is removed, because the adoption check is inside the unchanged `_held` call. Consequently the test cannot be the required regression test: with the diff reverted, `ON.apply` takes the identical code path for this input, so the test either passed before the change too (if `_held` already honoured adoption) or still fails after it (if `_held` does not, in which case the fix is incomplete and CI is red). The bug report explicitly requires a test that FAILS on the unfixed code; this one does not exercise any changed behavior.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_tree_dispose.py:73 (test_onboard_apply_never_removes_a_tree_an_item_adopted)

chunk_findings.detail: The stated bug is that *two* call sites, `services/cleanup.py:322` and `services/onboard.py:328`, remove worktrees without recording `worktree.removed`, so the fold's `item.worktree` goes stale, and the stated fix is that "all four call one `dispose_tree`". This diff contains no `dispose_tree` helper, no change to `api/lifecycle/merge.py`, `services/flow.py`, or `services/cleanup.py`, and only edits `onboard.py`. Therefore, if the report's premise about `cleanup` is correct, the defect it describes (after `cleanup` disposes a tree, the event log gets no `worktree.removed`, leaving `item.worktree` pointing at a deleted path) is entirely unaddressed by this change. At minimum the change does not do what its own description says it does.
chunk_findings.title: services/cleanup.py:322 (incomplete fix)

chunk_findings.detail: The diff only swaps the agent id used to construct one `EventLog`. It does not implement the fix the intent claims: nothing adds the log lock, the post-check claim re-check, or the `worktree.removed` logging around onboard's removal, and `cleanup.py` is not touched at all. Given the bug description ("onboard also removes with force and without the log lock, so it can delete a tree that an agent claimed between its check and the removal"), the race is still live in this change: release tree T, invoke onboard on T, and have another process claim/lease T in the window between onboard's existence check and its force removal — onboard still deletes T, leaving the claimant with a lease pointing at a deleted worktree. The changed line cannot affect that interleaving. Likewise the stated stale-fold symptom for cleanup (`cleanup.py:322` never logs `worktree.removed`) is untouched, so a tree removed by `ddflow cleanup` still leaves `fold`'s `item.worktree` pointing at the removed path. Closing B5e83fb22cb on this diff is premature.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/onboard.py:368 (the `effective_agent_id` change) / ddflow/services/onboard.py:328 (untouched removal path)

chunk_findings.detail: The added "regression test" does not exercise the bug it is supposed to guard. Its only assertion is `removed[-1].agent == "sweeper-7"`, i.e., that the `DDFLOW_AGENT` value is propagated into the removal event's agent field. It contains no check that the removal happened under the log lock, that the claim was re-checked, or that `fold`'s `item.worktree` was cleared. Input that demonstrates the gap: run this test on a build where onboard removes a tree that another process claimed mid-flight (or where cleanup removes a tree and never emits `worktree.removed`) — the agent-attribution assertion is unaffected, so the test passes while the reported defect is still present. It therefore cannot serve as the failing-then-passing regression test for B5e83fb22cb; at most it pins the incidental `effective_agent_id` behavior.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_tree_dispose.py:95 `test_the_removal_is_written_as_the_agent_ddflow_agent_names`

chunk_findings.detail: The reported bug B5e83fb22cb has two removal sites that must start recording `worktree.removed`: cleanup (`services/cleanup.py:322`) and onboard (`services/onboard.py`). The diff only edits `ddflow/api/onboard.py` and `ddflow/services/onboard.py`; `ddflow/services/cleanup.py` is not touched at all, and no shared `dispose_tree` (or equivalent log‑under‑lock emit) is introduced anywhere. Concrete case: take a repo with a merged, clean `Leftover` worktree and run `ddflow cleanup`'s removal path; after it completes, `EventLog(repo).read_all()` still contains no `worktree.removed` event, so `fold(...).item.worktree` remains stale — exactly the symptom the bug describes. The diff therefore leaves half of B5e83fb22cb unfixed while appearing to close it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/cleanup.py:322 (missing from the diff)

chunk_findings.detail: The new "regression test" asserts only `removed[-1].agent == "declared-3"` on an event that the pre‑fix onboard path already emits (the neighbouring pre‑existing test at lines 95‑99 shows `ON.apply` already produces `worktree.removed` with `agent == "sweeper-7"`). It never exercises the defect named in the bug: it does not run the cleanup path, it does not check that a removal ever gets recorded when none was before, and it does not attempt the claim/re‑check interleaving that the fix is supposed to guard (`onboard` removing a tree an agent claimed between the check and the removal). Consequently the test passes on any build that merely threads `--agent` into the identity field, regardless of whether the stale‑`item.worktree` defect or the TOCTOU race is actually fixed, so the bug can be closed with `--regression-test` without ever reproducing it.

Given `ts="1970-01-01T00:00:00Z"` (or the microsecond form `"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z"`, or any pre-1970 UTC timestamp such as `"1969-12-31T23:59:59.000000Z"`), `epoch(ts)` returns `0.0` (or a negative number), so `_age_s` returns `float("inf")` instead of the real age. chunk_findings.detail: The two sides of the comparison are now quoted differently. The changed-path set is read with `git status --porcelain -z`, which emits pathnames *verbatim* (no C-quoting at all), while the `diff` text is read with only `core.quotepath=false`. That setting only stops git from octal-escaping bytes with the high bit set; git *always* C-quotes backslash, double-quote and control characters, even with `core.quotepath=false`. So for a path containing `\`, `"`, or a control char the two representations no longer match, and `missing = [p for p in changed if p not in diff]` reports it as missing. Concretely: a tracked file named `a"b` (one double-quote) that is modified yields `path = 'a"b'` from `_status_paths`, but `capture_diff`'s output contains `a\"b` (git renders `diff --git "a/a\"b" "b/a\"b"`); `'a"b'` is not a substring, so `diff_covers_everything` returns `(False, ['a"b'])` even though the diff fully covers it. Same for a file named `a\b` (raw status `a\b` vs diff `a\\b`) and for tab/newline in a name. This is a regression rather than a pre-existing gap: before the change, status was read with default quoting and `strip('"')`, so both sides carried the same escapes (e.g. status `"a\"b"` → `a\"b`, which *is* in the default-quoted diff), and the old first-character bug did not affect quoted names because the eaten character was the opening quote. The fix only closes the mismatch for high-bit (non-ASCII) bytes while opening it for these always-quoted bytes.

chunk_findings.detail: The new failure test `then <= 0` conflates "the string could not be parsed" with "the timestamp is at or before 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z". The old code parsed the epoch instant successfully (`datetime.strptime("1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z", "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%fZ").timestamp() == 0.0`) and returned a finite age: `_age_s("1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z", now=1_790_000_000.0)` used to be `1_790_000_000.0`, and `_age_s("1969-12-31T23:59:59.000000Z", now=1_790_000_000.0)` used to be `1_790_000_000.0 + 1`; both now return `float("inf")`. That contradicts the function's own new docstring ("infinite when `ts` is not a timestamp") for inputs that *are* timestamps, and it only occurs because `epoch` apparently uses 0/negative as its parse-failure marker, so a legitimate pre-epoch value is indistinguishable from garbage. Practical impact is small (session records are modern), but any caller/test that treats `0.0`-valued timestamps as valid now sees "infinitely old"; if `epoch` instead signals failure with exactly `0.0`, the guard should be `then == 0.0` (or the sentinel should be checked via a distinct "parsed" result) rather than `then <= 0`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_status_paths` now reads status with `-z`, so it returns each file's byte-exact name, but the diff it is compared against is produced with only `-c core.quotepath=false`, and that option disables C-quoting *only for bytes > 0x80*. Names containing `"`, `\`, TAB or LF are still C-quoted by git in the diff (`diff --git "a/a\"b" "b/a\"b"`, `rename from a\nb`, etc.), so the raw status path is never a substring of the diff. Concretely, for a changed tracked file literally named `a"b`, `_status_paths` returns `a"b`, the diff contains only the escaped `a\"b`, and `missing = [p for p in changed if p not in diff]` yields `['a"b']`, so `diff_covers_everything` returns `(False, ['a"b'])` — falsely reporting a file that the diff does contain (same for a backslash or a newline/tab in the name). The pre-change code compared C-quoted-to-C-quoted (`.strip('"')` of the quoted status line matched the quoted diff header), so this is a regression introduced by switching only the status side to raw `-z` while leaving the diff output escaped; a truly raw comparison needs the diff read with `-z`/`--raw` too, not just `core.quotepath=false`.

chunk_findings.detail: `test_a_non_ascii_untracked_file_reaches_the_review_diff` calls `W.capture_diff(repo)` (line 49) and only afterwards asserts `"café.txt" in W.untracked_files(repo)` (line 53). Per the change's own description, `capture_diff` is what makes the non-ASCII name work by running `git add -N` on the listed untracked files. Once `git add -N café.txt` has run, the file is an intent-to-add entry in the index, so `git status --porcelain` reports it as ` A` (second column) rather than `??`, and `git ls-files --others` / a `??`-filtered status listing no longer contains it. `untracked_files()` therefore returns a list without `café.txt` (typically `[]`), and line 53 fails — i.e. this regression test cannot pass on the fixed code, only on the unfixed code (where `add -N` errored out and left the file untracked). The check of `untracked_files()` needs to run before `capture_diff`, or against a freshly created repo, to observe the raw (non-C-quoted) name.

chunk_findings.detail: `epoch()` returns `0.0` both for "not a timestamp" and for the legitimate Unix epoch, so the new equality sentinel `then == 0.0` still reports an infinitely old age for a valid timestamp — and `_age_s`'s own contract is "infinite when `ts` is **not** a timestamp". Concretely, `S._age_s("1970-01-01T00:00:00Z", now=THEN)` computes `then = 0.0`, the guard fires, and the function returns `float("inf")` instead of the true age `THEN`. The change deliberately taught the function that pre-1970 values are real (the added `test_a_timestamp_before_1970_has_a_real_age` asserts `1969-12-31T23:59:59Z` → `THEN + 1`), but stops exactly one second short of the boundary it claims to handle: `1969-12-31T23:59:59Z` is finite while `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` is infinite, an off-by-one-second discontinuity at the sentinel. The pre-existing test only covers genuinely unparseable strings (`"yesterday"`, `""`), so it does not pin down the sentinel and does not catch this. A sentinel that cannot collide with a real value (e.g. `epoch()` returning `None` for parse failure, or a separate "is a timestamp" predicate) is needed; otherwise the fix leaves the original bug class—"valid timestamp treated as infinitely old"—partially unaddressed at exactly the epoch.

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces the `then <= 0` guard with `then == 0.0`, treating 0.0 as `epoch`'s sentinel for "not a timestamp" while (correctly) letting negative values through as real pre-1970 timestamps. But `epoch` derives its value from the parsed instant, so the valid timestamp `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` (and its microsecond form `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z`) also produces exactly `0.0`. chunk_findings.detail: The new failure test `then <= 0` conflates "the string could not be parsed" with "the timestamp is at or before 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z". The old code parsed the epoch instant successfully (`datetime.strptime("1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z", "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%fZ").timestamp() == 0.0`) and returned a finite age: `_age_s("1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z", now=1_790_000_000.0)` used to be `1_790_000_000.0`, and `_age_s("1969-12-31T23:59:59.000000Z", now=1_790_000_000.0)` used to be `1_790_000_000.0 + 1`; both now return `float("inf")`. That contradicts the function's own new docstring ("infinite when `ts` is not a timestamp") for inputs that *are* timestamps, and it only occurs because `epoch` apparently uses 0/negative as its parse-failure marker, so a legitimate pre-epoch value is indistinguishable from garbage. Practical impact is small (session records are modern), but any caller/test that treats `0.0`-valued timestamps as valid now sees "infinitely old"; if `epoch` instead signals failure with exactly `0.0`, the guard should be `then == 0.0` (or the sentinel should be checked via a distinct "parsed" result) rather than `then <= 0`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/sessions.py::_age_s (the `if then <= 0:` guard)

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces the `then <= 0` guard with `then == 0.0`, treating 0.0 as `epoch`'s sentinel for "not a timestamp" while (correctly) letting negative values through as real pre-1970 timestamps. But `epoch` derives its value from the parsed instant, so the valid timestamp `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` (and its microsecond form `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z`) also produces exactly `0.0`. That collides with the sentinel: `S._age_s("1970-01-01T00:00:00Z", now=THEN)` returns `float("inf")` instead of `THEN`, i.e. a perfectly valid timestamp is still reported as infinitely old — the same failure mode the bug describes. The newly added regression test probes only the second *before* the epoch (`1969-12-31T23:59:59Z`), so the boundary itself is untested and the sentinel ambiguity survives. Either `epoch` needs to signal "unparseable" out-of-band (e.g. `None`/raising), or `_age_s` must distinguish parse failure from a legitimate 0.0 epoch value.

chunk_findings.detail: `ts.replace("Z", "+00:00")` only attaches a timezone when the string actually ends in `Z`. For any value without a UTC designator — exactly the "imported or hand-edited records" this commit says it is fixing — `fromisoformat` produces a *timezone-naive* `datetime`, and `datetime.timestamp()` on a naive value uses the **host's local timezone** (platform `mktime`). So `_age_s("2026-10-06T10:00:00", now=NOW)` returns `NOW - 1746000000` on `TZ=Asia/Kolkata` (naive 10:00 read as 04:30 UTC → age overstated by 19800s) but `NOW - 1759744800` on a UTC CI/production host — the same stored record yields a different age depending on the machine, and DST transitions make the mapping ambiguous. The pre-change code called the shared `epoch` reader, whose accepted forms all carry a UTC designator (the very reason it returned 0.0/inf for `...:00Z` in this bug), so a Z-less value was rejected as "not a timestamp" rather than silently reinterpreted through the process timezone. If Z-less values are meant to be treated as UTC (which the rest of the log format assumes), naive results must be normalized (`dt.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)`) or rejected; if they are not valid inputs, the function should still not silently depend on the host timezone.

chunk_findings.detail: The new guard `if then <= 0: return float("inf")` conflates a parse failure with a valid Unix timestamp at or before the epoch. Given `ts="1970-01-01T00:00:00Z"` (or the microsecond form `"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z"`, or any pre-1970 UTC timestamp such as `"1969-12-31T23:59:59.000000Z"`), `epoch(ts)` returns `0.0` (or a negative number), so `_age_s` returns `float("inf")` instead of the real age. The old implementation parsed the microsecond form successfully and returned `now - 0.0`; the new code makes it infinite. This directly reintroduces the reported symptom—a valid ISO timestamp treated as infinitely old—for an input the fix does not test. The added test only checks 2026 timestamps, so it passes while this valid input still yields `inf`.

chunk_findings.detail: `epoch()` returns `0.0` both for "not a timestamp" and for the legitimate Unix epoch, so the new equality sentinel `then == 0.0` still reports an infinitely old age for a valid timestamp — and `_age_s`'s own contract is "infinite when `ts` is **not** a timestamp". Concretely, `S._age_s("1970-01-01T00:00:00Z", now=THEN)` computes `then = 0.0`, the guard fires, and the function returns `float("inf")` instead of the true age `THEN`. The change deliberately taught the function that pre-1970 values are real (the added `test_a_timestamp_before_1970_has_a_real_age` asserts `1969-12-31T23:59:59Z` → `THEN + 1`), but stops exactly one second short of the boundary it claims to handle: `1969-12-31T23:59:59Z` is finite while `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` is infinite, an off-by-one-second discontinuity at the sentinel. The pre-existing test only covers genuinely unparseable strings (`"yesterday"`, `""`), so it does not pin down the sentinel and does not catch this. A sentinel that cannot collide with a real value (e.g. `epoch()` returning `None` for parse failure, or a separate "is a timestamp" predicate) is needed; otherwise the fix leaves the original bug class—"valid timestamp treated as infinitely old"—partially unaddressed at exactly the epoch.

chunk_findings.detail: For a record whose timestamp has no `Z`/offset (e.g. a hand-edited or imported record `"2026-10-06T10:00:00"`, or one written by a UTC clock that omits the suffix), `datetime.fromisoformat(...)` returns a naive datetime and `then = ....timestamp()` interprets it in the machine's local zone. On `TZ=Asia/Tokyo` the intended UTC instant is read 9 h early, so `_age_s` returns an age 9 h too large and a recent session can be pruned prematurely; on `TZ=America/New_York` it is read 4–5 h late and the session is treated as younger than it is, so it lingers. The pre-existing test and the new regression test only exercise the `Z` forms, so a CI box running `TZ=UTC` will never observe the discrepancy. The intended fix (routing through the shared reader, which normalizes to UTC) avoids this; the `try/except` also does not cover the `OverflowError`/`OSError` that `mktime`-based resolution of out-of-range naive dates raises on some platforms.

chunk_findings.detail:
The change is meant to fix bug B7ab10b58f2, which has two named symptoms: "drops the first character of the first path **and reports renames as missing**." The three added tests only ever produce a single-file `status` entry: a modified tracked file (`_commit` + `write_text("two\n")`), an untracked non-UTF-8 file, and a content-only case. None performs a rename, so the rename half of the bug is neither reproduced nor guarded.

This matters concretely because the fix switches `git.status`/`git.paths` to `-z`, and `-z` fundamentally changes rename records: `git status --porcelain -z` for a `git mv a.py b.py` emits `R  b.py\0a.py\0` — two NUL-separated path fields for one entry (old path plus new path), whereas the non-`-z` form was a single `R  a.py -> b.py` line. A `-z` parser that naively treats every NUL-delimited field as a path will consume `a.py` as a separate, unmodified path and report it as missing — the exact "renames reported as missing" symptom. No test exercises this, so the stated fix for renames can silently remain broken (or be newly introduced by the `-z` switch) while CI stays green. A regression test should `git mv` a tracked file, run `capture_diff`/`diff_covers_everything`, and assert `ok`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new guard `if then <= 0: return float("inf")` conflates a parse failure with a valid Unix timestamp at or before the epoch. Given `ts="1970-01-01T00:00:00Z"` (or the microsecond form `"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z"`, or any pre-1970 UTC timestamp such as `"1969-12-31T23:59:59.000000Z"`), `epoch(ts)` returns `0.0` (or a negative number), so `_age_s` returns `float("inf")` instead of the real age. The old implementation parsed the microsecond form successfully and returned `now - 0.0`; the new code makes it infinite. This directly reintroduces the reported symptom—a valid ISO timestamp treated as infinitely old—for an input the fix does not test. The added test only checks 2026 timestamps, so it passes while this valid input still yields `inf`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/sessions.py:_age_s

chunk_findings.detail: `epoch()` returns `0.0` both for "not a timestamp" and for the legitimate Unix epoch, so the new equality sentinel `then == 0.0` still reports an infinitely old age for a valid timestamp — and `_age_s`'s own contract is "infinite when `ts` is **not** a timestamp". Concretely, `S._age_s("1970-01-01T00:00:00Z", now=THEN)` computes `then = 0.0`, the guard fires, and the function returns `float("inf")` instead of the true age `THEN`. The change deliberately taught the function that pre-1970 values are real (the added `test_a_timestamp_before_1970_has_a_real_age` asserts `1969-12-31T23:59:59Z` → `THEN + 1`), but stops exactly one second short of the boundary it claims to handle: `1969-12-31T23:59:59Z` is finite while `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` is infinite, an off-by-one-second discontinuity at the sentinel. The pre-existing test only covers genuinely unparseable strings (`"yesterday"`, `""`), so it does not pin down the sentinel and does not catch this. A sentinel that cannot collide with a real value (e.g. `epoch()` returning `None` for parse failure, or a separate "is a timestamp" predicate) is needed; otherwise the fix leaves the original bug class—"valid timestamp treated as infinitely old"—partially unaddressed at exactly the epoch.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/sessions.py:141

chunk_findings.detail: For a record whose timestamp has no `Z`/offset (e.g. a hand-edited or imported record `"2026-10-06T10:00:00"`, or one written by a UTC clock that omits the suffix), `datetime.fromisoformat(...)` returns a naive datetime and `then = ....timestamp()` interprets it in the machine's local zone. On `TZ=Asia/Tokyo` the intended UTC instant is read 9 h early, so `_age_s` returns an age 9 h too large and a recent session can be pruned prematurely; on `TZ=America/New_York` it is read 4–5 h late and the session is treated as younger than it is, so it lingers. The pre-existing test and the new regression test only exercise the `Z` forms, so a CI box running `TZ=UTC` will never observe the discrepancy. The intended fix (routing through the shared reader, which normalizes to UTC) avoids this; the `try/except` also does not cover the `OverflowError`/`OSError` that `mktime`-based resolution of out-of-range naive dates raises on some platforms.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/sessions.py:_age_s

chunk_findings.detail: The new regression test calls `_time.tzset()`, which does not exist on Windows (and is missing from some non-glibc builds/Python builds). On those platforms the test does not exercise `_age_s` at all — it raises `AttributeError: module 'time' has no attribute 'tzset'` and errors the suite. Separately, the teardown path is not symmetric: `monkeypatch.delenv("TZ")` removes the env var and `tzset()` re-reads the *system default*, but `monkeypatch` restores the original `TZ` value at teardown without another `tzset()`, so the C library's cached timezone stays at the system default for the remainder of the process. If the test environment started with `TZ` set (e.g. `TZ=America/Los_Angeles` in CI), every later test that relies on local-time interpretation of a naive datetime sees the wrong zone. The test should skip when `tzset`/`TZ` are unavailable and re-`tzset()` after restoring the environment.

chunk_findings.detail: The new failure test `then <= 0` conflates "the string could not be parsed" with "the timestamp is at or before 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z". The old code parsed the epoch instant successfully (`datetime.strptime("1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z", "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%fZ").timestamp() == 0.0`) and returned a finite age: `_age_s("1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z", now=1_790_000_000.0)` used to be `1_790_000_000.0`, and `_age_s("1969-12-31T23:59:59.000000Z", now=1_790_000_000.0)` used to be `1_790_000_000.0 + 1`; both now return `float("inf")`. That contradicts the function's own new docstring ("infinite when `ts` is not a timestamp") for inputs that *are* timestamps, and it only occurs because `epoch` apparently uses 0/negative as its parse-failure marker, so a legitimate pre-epoch value is indistinguishable from garbage. Practical impact is small (session records are modern), but any caller/test that treats `0.0`-valued timestamps as valid now sees "infinitely old"; if `epoch` instead signals failure with exactly `0.0`, the guard should be `then == 0.0` (or the sentinel should be checked via a distinct "parsed" result) rather than `then <= 0`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/sessions.py::_age_s (the `if then <= 0:` guard)

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces the `then <= 0` guard with `then == 0.0`, treating 0.0 as `epoch`'s sentinel for "not a timestamp" while (correctly) letting negative values through as real pre-1970 timestamps. But `epoch` derives its value from the parsed instant, so the valid timestamp `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` (and its microsecond form `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z`) also produces exactly `0.0`. That collides with the sentinel: `S._age_s("1970-01-01T00:00:00Z", now=THEN)` returns `float("inf")` instead of `THEN`, i.e. a perfectly valid timestamp is still reported as infinitely old — the same failure mode the bug describes. The newly added regression test probes only the second *before* the epoch (`1969-12-31T23:59:59Z`), so the boundary itself is untested and the sentinel ambiguity survives. Either `epoch` needs to signal "unparseable" out-of-band (e.g. `None`/raising), or `_age_s` must distinguish parse failure from a legitimate 0.0 epoch value.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/sessions.py:141 (`_age_s`)

chunk_findings.detail: `ts.replace("Z", "+00:00")` only attaches a timezone when the string actually ends in `Z`. For any value without a UTC designator — exactly the "imported or hand-edited records" this commit says it is fixing — `fromisoformat` produces a *timezone-naive* `datetime`, and `datetime.timestamp()` on a naive value uses the **host's local timezone** (platform `mktime`). So `_age_s("2026-10-06T10:00:00", now=NOW)` returns `NOW - 1746000000` on `TZ=Asia/Kolkata` (naive 10:00 read as 04:30 UTC → age overstated by 19800s) but `NOW - 1759744800` on a UTC CI/production host — the same stored record yields a different age depending on the machine, and DST transitions make the mapping ambiguous. The pre-change code called the shared `epoch` reader, whose accepted forms all carry a UTC designator (the very reason it returned 0.0/inf for `...:00Z` in this bug), so a Z-less value was rejected as "not a timestamp" rather than silently reinterpreted through the process timezone. If Z-less values are meant to be treated as UTC (which the rest of the log format assumes), naive results must be normalized (`dt.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)`) or rejected; if they are not valid inputs, the function should still not silently depend on the host timezone.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/sessions.py — `_age_s`, the `datetime.fromisoformat(ts.replace("Z", "+00:00")).timestamp()` line

chunk_findings.detail: `datetime.UTC` was added in Python 3.11 only. The very code this patch touches still contains the idiomatic pre-3.11 workaround `ts.replace("Z", "+00:00")`, which is required precisely because `datetime.fromisoformat` on Python ≤3.10 rejects a bare `Z` suffix (and `UTC` is only importable from 3.11 on). On such an interpreter, `import ddflow.services.sessions` raises `ImportError: cannot import name 'UTC' from 'datetime'`, taking down every caller of the module, not just `_age_s`. The equivalent portable form is `from datetime import timezone` / `timezone.utc`. If the project truly pins ≥3.11 (making the `Z`-replace dead code), this is moot; otherwise it is a hard import-time failure.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/sessions.py:38 (`from datetime import UTC`)

chunk_findings.detail: The cleanup is wrong for the case where `TZ` was already set before the test. `monkeypatch.delenv("TZ")` in the `finally` removes the variable rather than restoring the original value, and the `_time.tzset()` that follows therefore installs the *unset-TZ* zone into the C library. `monkeypatch`'s teardown then puts the original `TZ` back into `os.environ` but never calls `tzset()` again, leaving libc's timezone out of sync with the environment for the remainder of the session. E.g. with `TZ=Europe/Berlin` in CI, after this test any later code that evaluates a naive `datetime.timestamp()` or `time.localtime()` silently gets UTC instead of Berlin time and produces an age/timestamp off by the offset. Secondarily, in environments without tzdata (minimal containers), `TZ=Asia/Tokyo` is ignored by `tzset()`, local time degrades to UTC, and the test then passes even against the unfixed code — i.e. it can stop being a regression test at all.

chunk_findings.detail: The two sides of the comparison are now quoted differently. The changed-path set is read with `git status --porcelain -z`, which emits pathnames *verbatim* (no C-quoting at all), while the `diff` text is read with only `core.quotepath=false`. That setting only stops git from octal-escaping bytes with the high bit set; git *always* C-quotes backslash, double-quote and control characters, even with `core.quotepath=false`. So for a path containing `\`, `"`, or a control char the two representations no longer match, and `missing = [p for p in changed if p not in diff]` reports it as missing. Concretely: a tracked file named `a"b` (one double-quote) that is modified yields `path = 'a"b'` from `_status_paths`, but `capture_diff`'s output contains `a\"b` (git renders `diff --git "a/a\"b" "b/a\"b"`); `'a"b'` is not a substring, so `diff_covers_everything` returns `(False, ['a"b'])` even though the diff fully covers it. Same for a file named `a\b` (raw status `a\b` vs diff `a\\b`) and for tab/newline in a name. This is a regression rather than a pre-existing gap: before the change, status was read with default quoting and `strip('"')`, so both sides carried the same escapes (e.g. status `"a\"b"` → `a\"b`, which *is* in the default-quoted diff), and the old first-character bug did not affect quoted names because the eaten character was the opening quote. The fix only closes the mismatch for high-bit (non-ASCII) bytes while opening it for these always-quoted bytes.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/worktree.py:_status_paths (used by diff_covers_everything)

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds `errors: str = "strict"` to `git()` and opts only the two `git diff` text calls into lenient decoding via `_diff_text`. Per the diff's own reasoning, `git()` already decodes strictly and "one such file aborted the whole review", yet every other git call in this file — in particular `untracked_files`, which the intent explicitly names, and the path listing in `capture_diff` — still calls `git()` without `errors`, and therefore now explicitly forces `errors="strict"`. So the fix only covers non-UTF-8 *content*; the enumerated file *names* are still decoded strictly. Concrete demonstration: create a worktree file whose name is not valid UTF-8 (e.g. bytes `b"caf\xe9.txt"`) and call `W.capture_diff(repo, include_untracked=True)`. `untracked_files` runs `git ls-files ... -z`; with `-z`, git emits the raw name bytes (no `core.quotepath` escaping), and `git()` decodes that output with the default `errors="strict"`, raising `UnicodeDecodeError` before `_diff_text` is ever reached — the review still aborts. The added regression test only exercises non-UTF-8 bytes in the file body with an ASCII name, so it passes while this path remains broken.

chunk_findings.detail: The change advertises fixing B7ab10b58f2 ("drops the first character of the first path … reports renames as missing"), but it does not touch the status parsing (`_status_paths`/`ln[3:]` at the line the bug description names) and it leaves `diff_covers_everything` deciding coverage purely by substring matching: `p in diff`, `_c_quoted(p) in diff`, `_c_quoted(p, raw_high=True) in diff`. Nothing anchors the match to a path/token boundary. So the exact failure mode described in the bug is still masked: if the first status entry is truncated (`café"b.txt` → `afé"b.txt`), then `changed == ['afé"b.txt']`, and `_c_quoted('afé"b.txt', raw_high=True)` produces `afé\"b.txt`, which is a suffix of the diff token `café\"b.txt`, so `diff_covers_everything` returns `(True, [])` and the file is reported as covered even though the real path never appears. The new regression test cannot detect this, because its only path is the one that gets truncated and truncation leaves a suffix of the real token; it fails on the old code only for the unrelated reason that the `raw_high` form is missing, not because of the first-character bug. Consequently the reported bug is neither fixed nor guarded — a name that is a suffix of a genuinely changed path (or a truncated first path) will always test as "covered".

chunk_findings.detail: `_c_quoted` only matches a path that git quoted *in full*, but the diff is no longer generated with the forced `-c core.quotepath=false`, so quoting now follows the user's config. With `core.quotepath=false` (a common user setting), git still escapes `"`, `\` and control bytes but emits high‑bit bytes raw, so a name that mixes a non‑ASCII byte with one of those (e.g. `café"b.txt`) is written as `"a/café\"b.txt"`: the path is neither present raw (`p == café"b.txt` is not a substring because a `\` intervenes) nor in fully‑C‑quoted form (`_c_quoted(p)` is `caf\303\251\"b.txt`, containing octal where the diff has the raw character). Such a covered file is falsely reported as missing. This is exactly the class of name the new docstring claims to match (`a"b` or `café`), but the combined case under non‑default `core.quotepath` is unhandled.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/worktree.py::_c_quoted / `missing` check

chunk_findings.detail:
The change is meant to fix bug B7ab10b58f2, which has two named symptoms: "drops the first character of the first path **and reports renames as missing**." The three added tests only ever produce a single-file `status` entry: a modified tracked file (`_commit` + `write_text("two\n")`), an untracked non-UTF-8 file, and a content-only case. None performs a rename, so the rename half of the bug is neither reproduced nor guarded.

This matters concretely because the fix switches `git.status`/`git.paths` to `-z`, and `-z` fundamentally changes rename records: `git status --porcelain -z` for a `git mv a.py b.py` emits `R  b.py\0a.py\0` — two NUL-separated path fields for one entry (old path plus new path), whereas the non-`-z` form was a single `R  a.py -> b.py` line. A `-z` parser that naively treats every NUL-delimited field as a path will consume `a.py` as a separate, unmodified path and report it as missing — the exact "renames reported as missing" symptom. No test exercises this, so the stated fix for renames can silently remain broken (or be newly introduced by the `-z` switch) while CI stays green. A regression test should `git mv` a tracked file, run `capture_diff`/`diff_covers_everything`, and assert `ok`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_diff_covers_everything.py (new tests, ~lines 63–85)

chunk_findings.detail:
`diff_covers_everything` decides "covered" by a substring search over the *entire* captured diff, and this change adds a third candidate spelling to that search. A changed path can therefore be accepted as covered even when it is not present in the diff at all, as long as the `raw_high` spelling occurs anywhere in the diff text — for example as a suffix of another, present path.

Concrete input: a repo with `core.quotepath=false`, containing `foo"cé.txt` at the root and `sub/foo"cé.txt` under a directory. Suppose the root file is changed but the captured diff omits it (precisely the situation this function exists to detect) while the sub-directory file is included. With `quotepath=false`, git emits the present path unquoted-high as `...b/sub/foo\"cé.txt...`. For the missing root path, `_c_quoted('foo"cé.txt', raw_high=True)` is `foo\"cé.txt`, which is a substring of `sub/foo\"cé.txt`, so the path is dropped from `missing` and the function returns `(True, [])` although `foo"cé.txt` is absent from the diff. The two pre-existing spellings do not match in this configuration (`p` = `foo"cé.txt` has an unescaped `"`; `_c_quoted(p, raw_high=False)` = `foo\"c\303\251.txt` has octal high bytes), so before this change the file was correctly reported missing. The new alternative makes the coverage check strictly more permissive and introduces a false-negative for `quotepath=false` repos that did not exist for that configuration.

chunk_findings.detail: The new drop does not go through `L.release` and is not gated on `[flow].claims`, unlike both `leases.release` (whose gating the helper docstring claims to imitate) and the new call in `services/identity.py`, which explicitly guards with `if cfg.flow.claims == "remote"`. On a repository that keeps the default local claims, resolving any contested item now invokes `L._remote_drop` for every loser even though remote refs are not in use. Showing the contrast: `identity.py` refuses to touch the remote unless claims are remote, while `resolve()` always does. Beyond the extra remote I/O, this is the exact path the bug description says must not bypass `L.release`, because `_transition` (and the event/transfer semantics) are still skipped even after the fix.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items.py:615-620 / 732 (_drop_remote_claims, resolve)

chunk_findings.detail: `L._remote_drop` is called unguarded, while the very next line wraps `L._remote_take` in `contextlib.suppress(L.LeaseError)`. If the drop raises a `LeaseError` (the same exception the neighbouring take is known to be able to raise — e.g. remote unreachable or the ref already reconciled), the exception propagates out of the re-homing function after the local `lease.released`/`lease.taken` events have already been appended. The result is a half-applied re-home: local state says `me` holds the item, the remote ref still names `bare`, and the remaining entries of `moved` never get their refs moved — i.e. precisely the failure the change claims to prevent, and the opposite of the stated "Best effort: a ref not moved lapses at its expiry" comment, which only holds for the suppressed take, not the drop.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/identity.py:113-117

chunk_findings.detail:
`_remote_claims` only switches the repo into remote-claim mode when the config file does **not** already contain a `[flow]` table. The ternary

```python
cfg.write_text(text + '\n[flow]\nclaims = "remote"\n' if "[flow]" not in text else text)
```

evaluates to `text` when `"[flow]" in text`, i.e. it rewrites the file byte-for-byte and leaves `flow.claims` at its default (`"local"`). So for any repo whose `.ddflow/config.toml` already has a `[flow]` section (for instance a config produced by the `repo` fixture or by an earlier test that persisted flow settings), remote mode is never enabled: `api.items.resolve` and the re-homing path take the local branch and never invoke `CR.drop`. Then `remote.calls` stays empty and both assertions — `assert ("drop", "T", "alice") in remote.calls` and `assert ("drop", "T1", bare) in remote.calls` — fail even on the fixed code, so the "regression test" does not actually exercise the remote-drop behavior under `flow.claims = "remote"` that the change is supposed to fix. The helper needs to insert/override `claims = "remote"` inside an existing `[flow]` table (or append the key) instead of returning the text untouched.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_release_paths.py:44 (`_remote_claims`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_in_diff_header` builds the needles `f"{lead}{side}/{path}"` but never requires the path to be terminated (by the closing `"` of a quoted name, a space, or end of the header). The left side is anchored only by the ` a/`/` b/` prefix, so a path that is a *prefix* of another path still matches, exactly as before. Given a worktree where `git status` reports changed = `["foo", "foo2"]` but the diff under inspection only contains `diff --git a/foo2 b/foo2 ...`, then `_in_diff_header(diff, "foo")` tests `" a/foo" in diff`, and `" a/foo"` is a substring of `" a/foo2"`, so it returns True. `foo` is therefore dropped from `missing` and `diff_covers_everything` returns `(True, [])` even though `foo` is genuinely absent from the diff — the precise silent-miss this guard exists to catch (`.gitignore` vs `.gitignore.bak`, `main` vs `main.py`, etc.). The docstring's claim that the match is "anchored" only rules out the tail case (`foo` inside `sub/foo`); the head/prefix case is still unhandled, so the fix does not actually make the coverage test sound.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/worktree.py:_in_diff_header

chunk_findings.detail: The final assertion `assert "café.txt" in W.untracked_files(repo)` is evaluated *after* line 52 has called `W.capture_diff(repo)`, and per this change's own intent text `capture_diff` registers untracked files with `git add -N` (the bug description literally says the non-ASCII name "breaks hash-object and add -N"). Once `git add -N` succeeds — which is exactly what the fix makes happen — `café.txt` has an entry in the index, so it is no longer reported by the untracked-listing query (`git ls-files --others` / the `??` status the `untracked_files` helper is built on). Concretely: on the unfixed code `add -N` fails for the C-quoted name, so the file stays untracked (but its listed name is C-quoted, so the assertion also fails); on the fixed code `add -N` succeeds, the file becomes intent-to-add and drops out of `untracked_files`, so the assertion fails as well. The regression test therefore cannot pass against the corrected implementation; the untracked check either needs to be taken before `capture_diff`, or the file has to be reset/removed from the index first.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_drop_remote_claims` is called unconditionally from `resolve`, and its drop loop (`for holder in holders: L._remote_drop(log, item, holder)`) is *not* gated on `cfg.flow.claims == "remote"`, even though the take in the very same function is (`if kept and cfg.flow.claims == "remote"`). Critically, `L._remote_drop(log, item, holder)` takes no `cfg`, so it has no way to self-gate on the claims mode; gating is the caller's responsibility. The sibling fix in this same change (`ddflow/services/identity.py:117`) does exactly that: it wraps *both* the drop and the take in `if cfg.flow.claims == "remote":`. So with the default/local claims configuration, resolving any contested item now walks `losers` and invokes the remote-drop path for every loser (e.g. item with two competing claims resolves -> two `L._remote_drop` calls against a remote that is not in use). At best this performs pointless remote work on every local resolution; if `_remote_drop` raises (`LeaseError` is evidently a realistic outcome, since the take right below is wrapped in `contextlib.suppress(L.LeaseError)`), the exception is not suppressed and propagates out of `resolve` *after* `item.resolved` has already been persisted, turning a successful local resolution into a reported failure. The drop loop belongs inside the same `cfg.flow.claims == "remote"` guard as the take.

chunk_findings.detail: The old adopt loop built the prompt-hook command explicitly and appended `" || true"` before handing it to `CH.install(...)`. The new loop delegates to `CH.install_spec(repo, h)`, and the `HookSpec` tuple listed in the intent — `HookSpec(agent, name, event, marker, file, matcher, flag)` — has no field that carries a shell suffix, so the `|| true` that used to force a zero exit status is gone. Concretely, running `ddflow adopt` with `claude` (and/or `gemini`) in `agents` now writes a `UserPromptSubmit`/prompt hook whose command is the bare `ddflow hooks ...` invocation. If that command exits non-zero — e.g. `ddflow` is not resolvable on the PATH Claude Code spawns hooks with, or the repo config it reads is missing/unreadable — the hook returns a non-zero status and Claude/Gemini treats the user's prompt as blocked/failed, whereas previously the `|| true` swallowed the failure and the prompt proceeded. This is a behavior change confined to the adoption path (the suffix was present in the exact lines being replaced), and nothing in the new spec-driven call restores it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt.py (prompt-hook install loop, replaced `cmd = ... + " || true"`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new fallback reads `h.purpose`, but the hook table's schema as defined by this change is `HookSpec(agent, name, event, marker, file, matcher, flag)` — there is no `purpose` attribute. Whenever `install()` is reached with a falsy `purpose` argument (exactly the path this fallback exists to serve — a caller that does not pass an explicit purpose), the generator evaluates `h.purpose` for the first matching row and raises `AttributeError: 'HookSpec' object has no attribute 'purpose'`. The failure is not benign ordering-wise: the call has already appended the group and executed `_write(path, data)` on the line above, so `.claude/settings.json`/`.gemini/settings.json` is mutated with the new hook while the caller still sees an exception (reported as failure, no return message, no rollback). If the intended source of the message text is the hook's `name` column, the reference should be `h.name`; if the field genuinely is `purpose`, the field list in the change description is wrong and the table constructor won't accept it.

chunk_findings.detail: The redirect note is appended *inside* the per-hook loop under `if h.name == "session-start"`, so its emission is keyed to every hook that happens to be named `session-start`, not to "the first hook" as the inline comment claims. The intent states the table covers `session-start` for `(Claude, Gemini)`; with such a table, running install with both harnesses selected iterates a Claude session-start entry and a Gemini session-start entry, and `msgs.append(note)` runs for each one that has a redirect, producing the note twice instead of once. The note's justification ("every line points where this one does") is also false for the Gemini entry, whose line points to the Gemini settings file while the Claude lines point to `.claude/settings.json`. A single note hoisted out of the loop (or guarded by an explicit "first emitted hook" flag rather than by name) is what "said once" requires.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py:_agent_hooks

chunk_findings.detail:
The removed loop built its command as `command_line(CH.PROMPT_MARKER, extra=..., refresh=...) + " || true"`, i.e. the prompt hook that got written into `.claude/settings.json` / Gemini settings was guaranteed to exit 0 even when `ddflow` itself failed. The replacement builds the command exclusively from the `HookSpec` fields that the intent enumerates (`agent, name, event, marker, file, matcher, flag`); none of those fields encodes the `|| true` suffix, and the only inputs `install_spec` can pass to `claudehooks.install` are the command derived from `marker`/`flag`, plus `event`, `marker`, `matcher`, `file`. So the suffix that the old code explicitly appended has nowhere to live in the new table.

Concrete failure: with a `ddflow` that exits non-zero for a `UserPromptSubmit` invocation (missing interpreter, broken config, a raised exception in the prompt handler), the previously installed command `... || true` swallowed the failure and the user never saw anything. After this change the installed command ends at the `ddflow ...` invocation, so every user prompt now returns a non-zero hook exit / surfaces hook stderr, which is exactly the behavior the removed `" || true"` was there to prevent. (If `install_spec` instead hard-codes `+ " || true"` for all specs, then this is not prompt-specific but the reverse regression: session-start/pre-compact hooks silently gain a swallow-all suffix they never had — either way the suffix handling is not preserved by the `HookSpec` table.)

Note: if `install_spec` is intended to hard-code the suffix for every spec, no finding applies to this hunk — that decision lives in part 1 and is not visible here.

chunk_findings.detail: The JSON branch that was deleted decided "unchanged" by full-entry equality: `get_server(data, target.shape, c.id) == server_entry_for(target.shape, c.entry())`. The replacement passes a single `same` predicate to `MC.register` for *all* shapes, and that predicate is `launches_as` — which the change's own comment describes as the TOML notion of identity ("a TOML entry is this companion when it LAUNCHES it (`launches_as`)"), i.e. it compares the launch command (command/args), not the whole stored entry. Because the shared writer is now fed the launch-only predicate for JSON as well, a JSON `mcpServers` entry that launches the companion the same way but differs in any non-launch field (`env`, an operator-added key, etc.) is now classified "unchanged" and left stale. Concrete case: companion `c`'s registry entry is `{"command":"npx","args":["-y","foo"],"env":{"TOKEN":"x"}}` and the repo's JSON config already holds `"foo": {"command":"npx","args":["-y","foo"]}`. The pre-change code sees `stored != server_entry_for(...)` and rewrites the entry (adding the `env`), so a subsequent `companions add` repairs it; after this change `launches_as` returns true, `register` reports "unchanged" ("already registers … with the same launch command"), and re-running `companions add` — the obvious remedy — silently does nothing, exactly the stale-entry failure the change claims to fix. This also contradicts the stated "byte-identical behaviour" for `companions.register`: equality to `want` is strictly stronger than launch-command equality, so any diff outside command/args that used to trigger a refresh no longer does.

chunk_findings.detail: This import previously bound the helper in this module's namespace as `toml_value`. The change rebinds it to the private alias `_toml`, so the name `toml_value` no longer exists in `companions`. Two concrete failures follow. (1) The comment claims the import is kept because the name is "re-exported": any existing consumer doing `from ddflow.services.companions import toml_value` now raises `ImportError`, whereas the sibling re-exports in the same diff (`_launch_of`, `_load_toml`, `_serves`, `_declared`, `_toml_without`) all deliberately keep their original names precisely so `from ...companions import <name>` keeps working. A re-export is only a re-export if the original name is preserved; aliasing it to `_toml` silently removes the public name. (2) Any code that remains in this module and calls `toml_value(...)` (the TOML serialisation callers of the re-exported `_declared`/`_toml_without`) now resolves an undefined name and raises `NameError`, because the only binding is `_toml`. The `# noqa: F401` even asserts the name is unused, which is exactly what makes the advertised re-export dead — the correct import is `from ..infra.tomlcfg import value as toml_value`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/companions.py (`from ..infra.tomlcfg import value as _toml`)

chunk_findings.detail: The removed JSON branch decided "unchanged" by exact structural equality of the stored entry against the desired one: `want = server_entry_for(target.shape, c.entry()); if get_server(data, target.shape, c.id) == want: return "unchanged"`, and only otherwise fell through to `place_server(... c.entry())`, which overwrites the entry wholesale. The replacement delegates every shape to a single `same` predicate, and the predicate supplied here is `launches_as`, which the new comment itself scopes to TOML ("a TOML entry is this companion when it LAUNCHES it (`launches_as`)"); the old JSON path never used it. For a JSON-shaped target (`target.shape != SHAPE_TOML`, e.g. `.mcp.json`) the stored value is a server object, so the "is this already right?" question is now answered by "does it launch the same thing" instead of "is it the desired entry". Concretely, a `.mcp.json` that already contains `c.id` with the companion's command/args but a stale non-launch field (e.g. an added `cwd`, a dropped key, or any field `launches_as` does not compare) is reported `unchanged` and never rewritten, where the removed code overwrote it via `place_server`. Re-running `companions add` — the documented remedy — then reports success while the JSON config keeps the stale entry, i.e. the exact "reported success and did nothing" failure the deleted comment warns about, and it contradicts the change's own claim that `companions.register` keeps "byte-identical behaviour" in the JSON case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/companions.py (companions.register, `same=lambda stored: launches_as(c, stored)`)

chunk_findings.detail: In `resolve`, the loser-release loop now calls `L.release_claim(log, item, holder=..., event=..., note=...)` and the post-transaction remote handling calls `L.settle_remote(log, cfg, item, dropped=..., kept=...)`. Neither of those is the API this change is supposed to introduce: the intent states that “every release, transfer and *loser release* goes through `L.release`”, and that the accepted fix for the duplicated remote drop-then-take is “Make it one `L.transfer`”. The symbols added in the companion parts are therefore `L.release` and `L.transfer`, not `L.release_claim`/`L.settle_remote`. Concretely: resolving any contested item (any `losers` non-empty) now evaluates `L.release_claim(...)` first, and even when `losers` is empty it hits `L.settle_remote(...)`; if those attributes are not defined on the leases module the call raises `AttributeError`, the `with log.transaction()` block never commits, and `resolve` fails instead of settling the item — while the previous code only used raw `log.append` plus the local `_drop_remote_claims` helper and therefore worked. If instead `L.settle_remote` does exist as a second helper, then the drop-then-take sequence is still implemented as a separate function from the `L.transfer` used by the identity re-homing path, so the duplication the change exists to remove is not actually removed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items.py:699-720 (`resolve`, the `L.release_claim` / `L.settle_remote` calls)

chunk_findings.detail: The old code performed the remote claim-ref move only when remote claims were actually in use, because the whole loop was wrapped in `if cfg.flow.claims == "remote":`. The replacement calls `L.settle_remote(log, cfg, item_id, dropped=[bare], kept=me)` unconditionally for every item in `moved`. If `settle_remote` is the thin consolidation of `_remote_drop` + `_remote_take` (which is what its name and `dropped`/`kept` arguments indicate — the `cfg` argument is needed for the git/repo plumbing, not for a mode check), then in the default local-claims configuration (`cfg.flow.claims != "remote"`) a B190 per-clone re-home of an item held by `bare` will now try to drop `bare`'s remote ref and take it for `me`, where it previously did nothing. In local mode those refs are never created, so the drop/take either writes spurious claim refs that no local-mode reader expects, or raises `LeaseError`; note that the old code deliberately suppressed `LeaseError` around `_remote_take` only, so error handling for the now-unconditional call depends entirely on `settle_remote`'s internals. Concrete scenario: `claims == "local"`, one item with `lease` held by `bare`, lock acquired, `moved = [item_id]` — old code logs the release/acquire pair and skips the ref move entirely; new code always invokes the remote settlement path. If `settle_remote` does re-check `cfg.flow.claims` internally this is a no-op and there is no defect, but nothing in the diff or the stated intent ("the remote-claim drop-then-take sequence is now written twice, in resolve and in identity re-homing") shows such a check being moved into the helper, and the call site lost the guard it previously had.

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds `release_claim`, which writes a `lease.released` event with a raw `log.append(...)` and never calls `L.release`. The stated goal of this series is that "every release, transfer and loser release goes through L.release", and the same intent note records the open bug "Raw lease.released appends bypass L.release (bug filed)" — this change adds a *new* bypass of that kind and leaves `release()` (defined immediately below, unmodified) as a second, independent release implementation. Concretely, when `transfer()` hands a claim from `holder` to `to`, or when `resolve` displaces a loser, the only effect is the raw `lease.released` append; any behaviour that lives in `L.release` and not in `release_claim` (its holder/operator-accepting signature and `bool` result, validation/dedup, remote-ref handling, and whatever fields `release()` puts on the event such as the claim's globs/expiry bookkeeping) is silently skipped for those two paths, so the two implementations can and will diverge — and the filed "bypass" bug is preserved instead of closed. Fix: have `release_claim` (or `release()`) delegate to the single `L.release` entry point for named claims rather than appending `lease.released` directly.

chunk_findings.detail: The predicate at this site was changed from the grace-aware `lease.expired(now, cfg.lease.grace_s)` to `not lease.live(now, cfg.lease.grace_s)`. The new `live` is `not (expired_at or expired(now, grace))` — the very definition confirmed by the property-test change in this same diff, which now requires `not i.lease.expired_at` for a lease to count as live. That means a lease which merely carries a recorded expiry (`expired_at` set) is reported non-live *even while it is still inside its grace window*, because `expired_at` short-circuits the time test. A recorded expiry is implemented by setting `ttl_s = 0` precisely so that the grace-based check keeps the lease active for `grace_s`; the old predicate respected that, the new one does not. Concrete input: a lease with `renewed_at = now - 1`, `ttl_s = 0` (recorded expiry), `expired_at` set, and `cfg.lease.grace_s = 60`. Here `lease.expired(now, 60)` is `False` (`1 <= 60`), so this item was previously skipped; `lease.live(now, 60)` is `False` (because `expired_at` is set), so the `not live` branch now fires and the item is treated as salvageable/removed while the agent is still legitimately within its grace window, i.e. work is reclaimed out from under a lease that the stated rule says "stays active for grace_s". The property-test oracle in this diff encodes the same grace-dropping definition, so the two changes agree with each other but not with the documented grace semantics.

chunk_findings.detail: The structural liveness scan exempts the whole of `core/records.py`. But the stated survey names `records.py:925 (active_leases)` as one of the three clock-only liveness checks (`expired(now, grace)` alone) that this change is supposed to eliminate. Because the file is on the allow-list, that call site (and any future raw `.expired(` added there) is skipped: leave `active_leases` as `if expired(now, grace): ...` and the loop appends nothing to `bad`, so the test that is supposed to guarantee "every liveness question goes through `Lease.live`" passes while the exact call site it was written for still bypasses the new API. The exemption is coarse (whole file) and lands precisely on the module the change targets.

chunk_findings.detail: The intent for this series is explicit: "every release, transfer and loser release goes through `L.release`", and the noted open bug is "Raw `lease.released` appends bypass `L.release`". The previous review's finding #3 established (and the author marked it **confirmed**) that the newly added `L.release_claim` writes the `lease.released` event with a raw `log.append(...)` and never calls `L.release`. This diff is exactly where `resolve` starts routing its loser releases through that helper — it replaces the old inline `log.append("lease.released", item, {...})` with `L.release_claim(log, item, holder=..., event=..., note=...)`. Nothing in the visible change makes `release_claim` delegate to `L.release`, and the probe cited for the triage (`test_release_claim_without_transfer_has_no_transfer_flag`) only pins that a bare `release_claim` sets no transfer flag; it does not make the loser-release path go through `L.release`. Concretely, resolving a contested item with a loser `H` still emits a raw `lease.released` append (bypassing `L.release`), so whatever release-side work `L.release` performs beyond the append is skipped for that loser even though the stated goal was to funnel all release paths through `L.release`.

chunk_findings.detail: `release_claim` still writes the `lease.released` event with a raw `log.append("lease.released", item_id, _released(...))` and never goes through `release()`, so `release()` (unchanged, immediately below) remains a second, independent release implementation with its own bookkeeping (`mine=False`, `holder=by`, `owner.update(holder=lease.holder)`). This is not answered by the change: the new `transfer()` — the function the intent says must be "one `L.transfer`" so that "every release, transfer and loser release goes through `L.release`" — calls `release_claim` first, i.e. `transfer(log, item_id, lease, to=..., now=...)` appends the release via this new bypass rather than via `L.release`. The cited probe, `test_release_claim_without_transfer_has_no_transfer_flag`, only asserts the presence/absence of the `transfer` key in the payload for `transfer=False`; it pins the payload shape, it does not route the append through `L.release`, so it cannot answer the finding. Concretely: any caller that relies on `release()`'s side effects (the `mine=False` attribution and the `owner.update(holder=lease.holder)` bookkeeping that a fold reading `lease.released` depends on) gets different event metadata for a transfer-release than for an ordinary release of the same claim.

chunk_findings.detail: The prior confirmed finding #3 is not answered by this diff. The probe test only asserts the *shape* of the event that `L.release_claim` emits — `"transfer" not in released.data and released.data["by"] == log.agent_id` — and that assertion passes identically whether `release_claim` delegates to `L.release(...)` or writes the `lease.released` event itself with a raw `log.append(...)`. So the test cannot distinguish "one release API" from "a second, independent release implementation". The diff reinforces the blind spot: the new AST guard in `test_no_caller_outside_the_lease_modules_reads_the_clock_or_writes_a_release` explicitly skips the whole of `services/leases.py` (`if path.name == "leases.py" and path.parent.name == "services": continue`) and so will never flag a raw `log.append("lease.released", …)` that lives in that module — which is exactly where the raw append added by `release_claim` lives. Concretely: if `release_claim` appends `lease.released` directly (as the change was reported to do) while `release()` remains an independent writer below it, every test in this file still passes, and the stated invariant ("every release, transfer and loser release goes through `L.release`") is unenforced. `test_release_claim_without_transfer_has_no_transfer_flag` should assert that the emitted event is the one produced by `L.release` (e.g. by monkeypatching/observing `L.release`), otherwise it pins the bypass rather than preventing it.

chunk_findings.detail: The condition changed from `lease is not None and not lease.expired(now, cfg.lease.grace_s)` (grace-only, no `expired_at` term) to `lease is not None and lease.live(now, cfg.lease.grace_s)`. The whole premise of the change is that `Lease.live` "honours `expired_at` everywhere", i.e. it is the `not expired_at and not expired(...)` form (that is exactly the semantics the unchanged items.py call sites at lines 148/169 encode). So for a lease whose expiry has been recorded (`expired_at` set, ttl 0) but which is still inside its grace window, the old expression evaluated to `live = True` (the `expired_at` flag was not consulted at this site) whereas the new one evaluates to `live = False`. Input: `lease.expired_at = now - 1`, `cfg.lease.grace_s = 60`, holder currently within grace — the guard that previously saw the lease as live now sees it as dead, so execution drops into the non-live branch (`if live ...` / fall-through). That is the opposite of the behaviour the change description itself documents ("A recorded expiry sets ttl 0 but the lease stays active for grace_s"), so an agent can act on / take over an item whose holder is still legitimately holding it for the remainder of grace. Since the intent says to "pin today's answers with a table test first", this site is a changed answer that the unification silently overwrites rather than preserves; either `live()` must reproduce the grace-only answer for this caller or the caller must be updated deliberately.
